#4174. Hot Wax sets fire to the Tetris playbook with slow-burn puzzle mechanics and a dollop of eldritch menace

Over the past couple of weeks, I've been conscious of an eerie background humming and hissing. For a while I thought it was just tinnitus, brought on by one too many listens of Control's Ashtray Maze OST, but then I realised that it was actually RPS regular quasiotter whispering in my ear about Hot Wax, which launches on Steam this week after a spell of Itch.io exclusivity.

It's the new arcade puzzler from PUNKCAKE Délicieux, otherwise known for inflicting shotguns on chess and forcing the alphabet to wear trousers in the name of archaeology, somehow. Hot Wax is actually quite straightforward by PUNKCAKE standards. It's Tetris, but all the blocks are candles, and rather than filling a line on the grid to clear blocks, you have to plant unpredictably dropped flames on wicks to slowly sizzle the mass away. Relatively straightforward, yes, but fiddly in practice. Did I mention that you're doing all this in a temple, under the eye of a "not unfriendly" eldritch god?

There's still a demo for Hot Wax on Steam, with the full release due in Valve's cathedral of commerce tomorrow. I've had a go at that demo, and it has tickled my brain. You need to line up candles, wick to wick, rather than just filling gaps, as in Tetris. But you still, ideally, need to avoid gaps to slow down the filling of the screen. Once a wick is lit, it'll gradually melt the candle and leap to any other wicks it touches.

Once a candle is lit, you have to avoid smothering it by unscientifically dunking another candle on top of it, while trying to take advantage of how the melting wax alters the layout. I found this enjoyably challenging. And then there are the power-up items, acquired by sacrificing flames to the aforesaid "not unfriendly" god. These include bombs that light a bunch of wicks at once, and acorns that sprout a column-filling sapling. Not sure what they worship in this temple, exactly, other than Tetris.

There will be a bunch of modes in the full release – from basic score attack and endless play, to a mode where you have to melt several, painstakingly arranged candles with just one flame. They're also planning daily seeded challenge runs. As with PUNKCAKE stuff at large, it's a looker, with some lustrous pixel art and lots of nifty little animations. Thank you, quasiotter – this was fun! You can stop going "EEEEEEEE" in my ear now.

Unlock Master Chief, liveries and the Xbox IKEA Prop Pack!

Yesterday marked the long-awaited arrival of Forza Horizon 6's City Life update, which adds two new permanent race routes in Tokyo City amongst other things, and there are even some Xbox and Halo-related freebies tucked in!

In terms of Halo, it's said that everyone will soon be getting a free 2025 GR GT Prototype livery via the Message Centre celebrating the franchise along with Xbox's 25th anniversary. #4172. Subnautica 2 dev thinks early access teams should worry less about adding features that are "very ugly, incomplete, or prototype"

But acknowledges that "early access" ain't what it was

Subnautica 2 creative director Anthony Gallegos has spoken about what Unknown Worlds have learned over their many years working in Steam early access, exhorting other devs to add new features "as soon as possible" and experiment with them right under the flared nostrils of players. Damn the torpedoes, etcetera.

The original Subnautica is one of the oldest Steam early access success stories, launching in 2014 a month or so after the program went live. Many of the final version's better qualities, including the pivot to horror epitomised by the spectacle of a Reaper grabbing your submarine's face, reflect observation of players and streamers in the wilds.

"Subnautica often launched features when they were very ugly, incomplete, or prototype," Gallegos commented, as part of a group chat about early access with GamesIndustry.biz. "This gave fans a real sense of getting to see game development in progress, in a way few other studios would try, especially for a franchise as big as this."

Unknown Worlds have "cultivated a very empathetic audience through radical transparency," Gallegos continued. "We trust the audience to give us a little grace as we figure things out, and they in turn trust us to make it great in the fullness of time."

Naturally, Gallegos thinks it's vital to keep talking to players and taking their feedback on the chin. "Be honest with them and make them understand how crucial they are to the process," he went on. "Preserve your vision, but listen to them and let them help you bring the best out of your game." Early access remains "core" to the "DNA" of Unknown Worlds, as they continue with the creation of Subnautica 2, which is about to get a nourishing injection of robot frogs.

I'm writing this up mostly because I'd like to know where you all stand as regards the "very ugly, incomplete, or prototype" - which, now that I think about it, sounds like the film Sergio Leone might have made, if he'd gotten into industry documentaries rather than spaghetti westerns. My view on early access is basically that it has become the same things as live service. I'm not sure there's a meaningful division any more between labelling a game "unfinished" and the expectation that devs will keep adding stuff to any release.

Within that, though, there's a lot of diversity, as Gallegos acknowledges in the GI piece. "Early access could mean a game like ours doing long-term open development, or it could be a game three months from a 1.0 release that's effectively doing a paid beta soft launch and using the Early Access term as a way to soften player expectations," he observed.

Not everybody has been as fortunate as Unknown Worlds in persuading players to give them the benefit of the doubt. In a crowded market (GI say that 2,924 early access games have launched on Steam this year so far, citing SteamDB), newer teams may suffer from being compared to older operators like Unknown Worlds, who got involved when early access was still fresh and exotic.

Elsewhere in the GI article, Denis Dyack, CEO of Deadhaus Sonata developer Apocalypse Studios, argues that expectations are unavoidably set by the early access devs with the largest budgets, citing Subnautica 2 as an example.

Back to you, the atrocious buyer of unfinshed games: what do you expect from an early access release? What degree of wobble will you overlook? What are you happy for devs to leave out till the final version? How important is communication, really? Does it just depend totally on the game? Here is some topical music to think along to.

#4171. Forza Horizon 6 explodes on Steam even before it's officially out

Forza Horizon 6 looks to have easily delivered the most successful launch for any game in the series on PC, with record-breaking player numbers.

Steam is abuzz this week with a couple of long-anticipated launches, but in Forza Horizon 6’s case, at least, the game isn’t even out for what will be most of its players. The anticipated sequel in the open-world driving game series doesn’t officially launch until May 19, but owners of its most expensive version - the Premium Edition - can play it right now.

That version of the game includes more than just a few days of early access, of course, but you’d think the $120 price tag would’ve only been palatable to a small group of players. Not the case with this game.

Forza Horizon 6, which has spent 16 weeks in Steam’s global top sellers list, currently occupies the number two spot, having jumped up three spots this week in anticipation of the launch. The game has also naturally been popular with players, so popular in fact that it has already overtaken the player counts of all other Horizon games on the platform.

At the time of writing, the game has peaked at 128,157 concurrent players on Steam alone (via SteamDB). The figure has already climbed several times during the writing of this story, so you can only imagine how much higher it’s going to get deeper into the weekend.

All of that, of course, days before the official launch on Tuesday, when, theoretically, the majority of the game’s audience will be able to start playing. In just a few short hours, Horizon 6 has already gone well above Forza Horizon 5’s peak concurrent of 81,096, as well as Forza Horizon 4’s peak 75,689 players.

Steam is the only platform that publishes player numbers, of course, but it’s easy to see how similar the enthusiasm is going to be on Xbox. Though the game is not yet part of the Game Pass line-up, those who don’t want to wait could buy the Premium Edition Upgrade to get the included content, and play it right now.

Game Pass, and Xbox / Windows Store numbers don’t factor into Steam’s, which is another thing to consider when viewing the numbers holistically. Indeed, given how successful Forza Horizon 5 has been on PlayStation 5, Horizon 6’s upcoming release on Sony's console is bound to be even bigger.

Forza Horizon 5 has been off to a similarly flying start in the first few days of its own advanced access launch, so it’s obviously not surprising to see Horizon 6 do better there. In case you missed it, check out our review of Forza Horizon 6. In short, we really liked it, even if we expected more.

It's here. It's finally here, and we'd wager you've spent a good chunk of the past 48+ hours playing it. Or perhaps you're savouring the moment, waiting for the perfect time to settle down with the most critically acclaimed game of the year (so far).

Either way, Ocarina is out on Switch 2, and millions of you have had the opportunity to dive into this beautifully reimagined version of a Hyrule that's near and dear to so many of us.

As mentioned, it's gone down very well with critics and currently sits with a whopping great Metascore of 96 after 85 reviews. Our own Ollie Reynolds called it "a remarkable remake, and a must-buy for Switch 2" in his 9/10 review:

"Ocarina of Time on Switch 2 is a stellar reimagining of the original, one that completely revamps the experience with stunning visuals, modernised gameplay, and vastly improved audio. Despite some minor blemishes, this is comfortably the most visually stunning work Nintendo has ever put out, and it’s unquestionably the best way to play one of the most seminal games of all time."

Review The Legend Of Zelda: Ocarina Of Time (Switch 2) - A Stunning Remake, But Not Quite Definitive

Now that the game has been out a couple of days, though, it's time to start canvassing public opinion: What score would you give this particular OoT?

No worries if you haven't played it yet or don't feel comfortable scoring it right now - you can return and rate the game at any time by revisiting this page or heading to our game page. As quickly as Ocarina veterans may have bolted through it, this is still a sizeable adventure, especially if you never played the original!

OoT 2026 is a 10/10 for me. It is an experience, not a game. The tightrope balance of keeping the feeling (cinematic and scope) while still amazing (as in to make someone amazed) the player is being well kept. There are areas of the game that make me viscerally uncomfortable (or elated) even though I know they are there.

This game is what nostalgia truly means. Not some ruined or derided longing for better days, but the ability to have core memories and associations strummed by an evocative experience. This game does this as I find myself giggling or shuddering or laughing or trying not to tear up. At the same time it is FUN. I miss pure adventure games in a world of open world procedurals (BOTW and TOTK managed to avoid this feeling), get gud death runs, and epic rpgs where I need a spreadsheet to keep track of choices made so I get the ending I want. I just want to wander, and perhaps find some new connection.

I’m reminded of why I was so adamant that zelda games were adventure games and not RPGs as a kid (I still feel this way), I don't need to learn combos but attack patterns are engaging enough that I am not playing a QTE, I can wander and discover and while there is a sense of danger, I don’t have to inch my way through, terrified that something is gonna spawn, stab my character and take away my progress. I can smile and be curious about the varied NPCs and make up little thought about their inner lives without having the game having to keep a realistic schedule. Also, oddly enough and I hate to say this, no romance. Just two kids chosen by destiny to stop a big bad in a world of magic. (I know there are shippers in every fandom. I don’t see it, so leave me alone). The presentation is beautiful, the gameplay and control design smooth and with no technical issues It feels like the storytelling quirks of all the Zelda games were neatly layered on to make the characters feel more vibrant, while leading with OoT’s narrative style.

It’s odd. As much as I loved OoT as a kid/adult, I didn’t think it a masterpiece…and felt it was a little bit of a sacred cow, even as I have replayed it many times. Yet this new version with its thrilling music, intuitive UI, engaging but constantly moving narrative style and beautiful but whimsical graphics I now get what people meant by this being a masterpiece instead of a very good game. If BOTW was LoZ (first game) fully realized, then this S2 OoT is OoT fully realized. It feels like a memory, it feels like a reunion, it feels like a link to the future. It is the best way to play OoT. What a time to be a Zelda fan.

I’m looking at the game as a first-time player, even though I am old enough to remember getting it on Xmas morning and playing it so many times over the years. It’s a rewarding experience for a new-comer and also someone like me who is appreciating all the flourish that was breathed into an old game. Little details I’ve noticed so far: the reactive fog on the ground in some areas is incredible. I think we can now move on from ooh-ing and aww-ing over water physics and now the new standard is ground fog.The other really cool detail I noticed is when picking up dungeon maps, while it’s floating over your head after you pull it out of the chest, the map depicted on the map is actually that current dungeon’s map, and it’s not just some re-used boilerplate sprite each time. They didn’t have to do that but they did and it’s just another small detail showing why Nintendo is the best as what they do.

It's a gorgeous remake. If you're a newcomer to the game, I'd call this a 8.5/10 - with the only issue being how weirdly handhold-y it is. I just finished the Zora's Domain area, and holy crap, it is absurd how much the game spells out exactly what to do. First they put a Zora holding a bottle in around the fish area, then they have the signpost in Zora's fountain literally saying "give an offering to Jabu," then a pool of water directly in front of Jabu, perfect for a fish. Any one of these hints would have been enough, but all 3? Overkill. If you have played the game before, I'd score it an 8, since the handhold-y bits wouldn't bother you (you know exactly what to do anyway). It feels a lot like taking a riding a Rollercoaster you've already ridden before. Very enjoyable, but the thrills are milder. I dock an extra half point because I think the devs could have added more stuff to celebrate the re-release (dev commentaries, concept art, old TV commercials, etc.). I also think the soundtrack is mixed weirdly. Certain instruments are way way too loud, and so the atmosphere in some places isn't as strong as it could be.

The wider gaming community would probably not consider static NPCs just standing around (or walking in circles), loading screens, pour voice acting, hand holding, and over all short gameplay, to be Peak gaming in 2026. (Nor would they be excited over a djump button)

It's a good game, I enjoy it a lot, but it's not a perfect 10.

@HexagonSun "I hope Super Mario 64 is next." Would be good if the added in all the 3ds stuff. New levels and characters to play as.

Honestly, this is one of those rare perfect games for me. Every change to the original is something that I can get behind, and the game as a whole is genuinely rekindling my love for the series itself. I've been falling out of Zelda this past decade due to the countless Warriors games and the way that the team seems to want to prioritize absolute freedom over all else. To a point where it's outright detrimental to the game design.

Also, it's just nice in general seeing this game get such a massive graphical face-lift like this. It's gotten me to want a Majora's Mask remake that's on the exact same level in terms of visuals, along with story changes that heighten everything.

10/10. I didn't really love the OG for it being too childish at the time. This version finally made me fall in love with the game. I'm 49.

@TrogdorTheBurninator Your average gamer wants an open world game with hundreds of hours of filler content, so yeah it probably wouldn't be a perfect 10/10 if it were on other platforms. Look at how many people are drooling at the mouth for a game like GTA6, which is more than likely just overhyped garbage.

I'm just glad that I get to experience a well done remake of a game with hand-designed content that's intentionally designed. I also don't really get where the "hand-holding" complaint comes from, because the game cuts a lot of the tutorial stuff from the original Ocarina of Time down. Navi doesn't sit and explain how to solve puzzles anymore.

I've only completed the first Dungeon and learnt a handful of songs so it's probably too early to tell but for me, this is feeling like it's going to be an easy 10. Experiencing an all-time classic like this feels truly magical in a way I can't quite compare to any other game I've ever experienced. Maybe that's not the most objective critique but if games are art, then I'm going to let the way it makes me feel serve as my guiding compass for a numerical score.

@VoidofLight If it's not Navi, it's the owl or Impa showing up to tell you where to go next.It's a preference thing, BOTW nailed it imo. I do not want to take away from your 10/10 experience, I'm just a bit surprised so many people find it flawless.

Reached the Zora village and I'd give it a 9.t’s an amazing game, and I’m loving every minute of revisiting it. The sense of adventure is as magical as ever, and the music is incredible (I can easily see the score winning awards).

The graphics are nice and all but since I’ve been switching between Phantom Blade Zero and OoT, the remake feels quite modest visually by comparison, which takes the edge off the “wow” factor. The original was cutting-edge for its time, so part of me keeps wishing for that same jaw-dropping moment. It makes me curious what Nintendo could dream up on even more powerful hardware!

Lost visual impact aside, I agree with the NL review: it plays things on the safe side, but it’s such a charming journey that I don’t mind too much. I’d have loved a sprinkle of BotW/TotK magic in Hyrule Field, and more voiced cutscenes, since the ones included are so beautifully done.

All the comments about the voice acting are sadly confirming one of my biggest worries. I hope Nintendo adds an option to mute spoken dialogue. Until then, I might pass on this. :/

I've seen the Pixies perform "Doolittle," Ween perform "The Mollusk," and Public Enemy perform "It Takes A Nation Of Millions To Hold Us Back."

Legendary acts, but each was kinda predictable tbh. (P.E. was the best by far, but also I was the least familiar with that album at the time. Does anyone see what I'm getting at, here? ✌️)

@Bustacap yeah, I meant DS. Dunno why I put 3DS lol.

I completed the game fully about half an hour ago. I’ve been visiting this site for years but have never made an account, but after playing this felt compelled to.

I’m going straight in to say I gave this game a 10/10 - I can’t quite believe what I’ve just experienced. I have so many emotions, thoughts, feelings coursing through my body and mind, I’m not quite sure I can say anything coherent.

This was my first Zelda game which I played in 2000 when I was 11. It captivated me then and never let go; I have revisited this game at least once per year ever since, including the incredible 3DS version. I was one of those who longed for this remake and to say it delivered and exceeded expectations is an understatement.

When the trailers were first revealed, I wasn’t sure about the character models and the English voice acting (American accents, ugh, I agree with the other poster who said that they just don’t fit this epic/heroic/mythological type stories, whether movies or games). Thankfully, the remake allows you to play with the Japanese voice actors which I changed the game to as soon as I was able (hearing Navi with that preppy American speak I so detest was an instant nope). The voice acting was sublime in Japanese and really drew me into the world.

And what a world! The game is beyond gorgeous, and I found myself smiling so many times throughout; I also gasped, laughed, chuckled and had a little cry at times (I had a big cry during the end!). The original Ocarina of Time was a straight 10 for me, and this is the same game, just remade in 2026. There has been much criticism that it plays too safe, but I wanted Ocarina and that’s what I got. There were just enough changes that some small parts were new and unfamiliar which I found very enjoyable, and I enjoy all the changes. I loved being able to walk into Lake Hylia and Lon Lon Ranch without loading screens, and having night versions of some of the tracks was a cherry on top.

The soundtrack! It is magnificent; I have no other word to describe it. OOT is one of the greatest soundtracks ever created in gaming, and this versions arrangements elevate and enhance what was already stellar.

One of the strongest aspects of the original Ocarina was the atmosphere, and I was overjoyed to discover that this version perfectly portrayed the atmosphere, again in some places enhancing it. It’s strange how often I truly felt that this was the game as I’d always played it, despite knowing that wasn’t true. There will always be room in my life to revisit the N64 and 3DS versions from time to time, but henceforth this is the definitive version (I am slightly baffled that NL reviewer said it isn’t the definitive version, perhaps due to the lack of Master Quest, but as someone who has never played Master Quest beyond Dodongo’s Cavern, it was no loss to me).

I think the reason why Ocarina of Time captivated and stayed with me since the day I started playing it is because it truly does feel like a legend. The archetypal story of good vs evil is done superbly in Ocarina, and no matter which version I’ve played, it always feels epic, heroic and legendary. I’ve seen many reviewers say that perhaps this version isn’t made for “us”, “us” being older gamers who were there from the beginning, however, I don’t agree; this legend belongs to us all, and I hope that when I’m long dead and gone, people will still be telling the legend of the Hero of Time.

1. It feels 3x faster than the original, because it is, 2. coupled with the incredible sound and music,3. upgraded visuals to the nth degree.. 4. And given the magic of the original

All of the above combined and this is the ultimate ocarina of time experience. Speechless...

I finished the game just now, and I just wish the game was handled a bit more.... grand? I think? Like we've already had a 1-to-1 remake with the 3DS version. Obviousy this Switch remake isn't 1-to-1, but it's still really close, and I do wish they had expanded that scope a bit more.

For what it was though.... I still really really enjoyed it, and I absolutely do not regret buying the game. Ocarina of Time is and always will be one of the best video games ever made, and this remake can count itself among that for sure. Just, because it played it a bit too safe, I can only give it a 9 out of 10 for that reason, even if I feel like it's a 10 out of 10 like the original was.

I gave it a 9, because it's a super pretty version of one of the best games ever. I'm not too far in so far, about to start Dodongo Cavern.

It's nice that it brings back that 90's nostalgia and is by far the prettiest Nintendo game ever. Also making me realize more of what the open world Zeldas need to incorporate in the future - a more detailed and narrative experience, and of course dungeons.

Having a great time playing it. But still it is a very safe remake. I would have loooooved if they had made it with the idea of "OoT but if it was made today", rather than basically a 1-to-1 remake. That woulda been a 10 for me.

Heck even if all they did was rebuild the combat and enemy AI from the ground up according to high modern standards to make combat and bosses wayyyy more interesting and more difficult, while also expanding some key areas, for example make Hyrule Field like >5x bigger and fill it with interesting places to explore and things to do so that it would be a whole little mini-world full of adventure, to bring the game closer to what an epic adventure game these days has, that woulda been a 10 for me.

So it's great cuz it's incredibly gorgeous OoT, but loses a bit from the disappointment of sticking exactly to what was cutting edge three decades ago rather than upgrading it (while keeping the same bones) into something that will wow people today. It's a safe and beautiful remake of a legendary game, so deserves a high score, but definitely a significant missed opportunity to do something more with it while they were going to the trouble of remaking the whole game.

Upon further reflection, I think another reason I loved playing this remake so much was because it showcases what I’m desperately missing - condensed, no nonsense, straight to the point gaming. As much as I genuinely adore BotW, Skyrim, the ancient Assassins Creeds, Super Mario Odyssey etc I’m so burned out on almost never ending games with an almost overabundance of things to do. Coming back to Ocarina of Time this weekend I had just finished playing Fenyx Immortals Rising and whilst I thought that another superb open world game, the tightly packed Ocarina felt like a breathe of fresh air and I missed this kind of game more than I’d realised. Perhaps moving forward game developers can come to some sort of middle ground, or even fully embrace the idea that not every game needs to last 50-100 hours plus to be incredible; there is so much room and I believe so much desire for these more contained experiences that have a definitive ending.

@TrogdorTheBurninator The game isn't open world, and that's what you're basically taking issue with. You don't like games that have stories or give you directions on where to go, but that doesn't make the game worse because it shows you into a specific direction- and there's still times where the game doesn't really point you in any direction at all (particularly the Spirit Temple, where you have to basically figure out where to go on your own).

Breath of the Wild wasn't really an amazing experience for me. The game was primarily filler content to pad out play time, and put it on the player to make their own fun rather than giving the player actual meaningful or well designed content to play through. Tears of the Kingdom only further doubled down upon that approach.

@ABmajora With how long console gens are getting these days (fully expect Switch2 to be around for 10 years until the next system) I wouldn't mind 3 Zeldas per gen. The main game as an epic open world masterpiece that always tries to push the bounds of Zelda and gaming in general, a smaller more directed old style of 3D Zelda, and a classic style 2D Zelda. Three Zeldas every 10-12 years, but with each one very different.

Bizarre that everyone was up in arms about Pokémon Firered/leafgreen costing 30$ each but they’re gushing over the Ocarina rehash which costs 85-100$ (plus the cost of the Switch 2).

@Euler It's because Fire Red and Leaf Green were ports of the original games upcharged, while this is a full on remake made from the ground up of one of the most important games of all time.

Also, I assume you're going off of Canadian prices, because the game is 70 USD for a physical copy, and 60 for a Digital copy.

@VoidofLight a rehash is a rehash is a rehash. The amount of new content is what counts, not how shiny the graphics are or how much dev time it ate up. And the Pokémon games were updated too; they added in three new Pokémon and fixed a game-breaking glitch.

@Euler The work put into the game actually does count! Contrary to your beliefs!

Also they did include extra content. They added tons of new cutscenes that flesh out the story, and tons of new music that never existed in the original game. Most of the dungeons and bosses got massively revamped as well.

@VoidofLight that’s just wasted resources that could’ve and should’ve been put into a new game. The dungeon changes are negligible. And there is not 85$ worth of new content, which is what they are charging for it. In fact the lack of master quest means there is actually less content than the 3ds version. But they’ll eventually rerelease the second half for another 30$ or so, if the rumours are to be believed.

@VoidofLight Every change is something you can get behind? What about all the puzzles/dungeon designs that were dumbed down/simplified, and most parts of the original that posed a challenge getting nerfed?

@Euler "That's just wasted resources that should've and could've been put into a new game."

They're working on a new game, chill. The resources aren't wasted, and if you read the developer interviews you'd know why this remake exists to begin with. It's a training exercise for the newer staff that joined the team that's meant to teach them the importance of Ocarina of Time to the Zelda series as a whole.

"Aonuma: This year marks the 40th anniversary of the very first Legend of Zelda game. With that in mind, I was thinking about what I should create as the producer of the series. Many of the team members who work alongside me on Legend of Zelda games today have only experienced developing the more recent titles. That led me to wonder, “Do they truly understand just how significant The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time was to the series as a whole?” Of course, there are team members who vaguely know the game, and those who played it in their childhood days. But I started to wonder how they'd interpret The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time as they go about developing future Legend of Zelda games. By learning the game structure and development style behind the original The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, and by actually rebuilding it as a full remake, it may trigger new insights that they can carry forward into future development. If we could achieve that, I thought it would be incredibly valuable. That’s what led us to the conclusion that now is the right time to revisit The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time once again." - Ask the Developers Vol. 24 The Legend of Zelda Ocarina of Time Part 1.

The dungeon changes aren't "negligible." They actively changed the flow of the game along with how puzzles operate. They actively fixed things like the Water Temple, which in all other versions of Ocarina of Time is notorious for not being fun and being confusing. They made bosses like Morpha actually have proper attacks.

This was a warranted revisit to the series.

As for Master Quest, we don't know if they're even going to charge for it. StarFox got a free update months down the road that added in online gamemodes, so it's more likely that Ocarina of Time's remake is going to have the same thing for Master Quest. It would be odd if they charged for DLC of a remake, and if they did- I don't think Master Quest is even really worth being paid DLC. It's effectively just a worse version of the base game and a bad ROM Hack. It would need a full on remake to be worth playing in and of itself.

@VoidofLight The handholding complaint is because tons of puzzles in the remake were made much simpler and/or have additional hints making it obvious what you have to do.

@Durians There weren't many puzzles that were "dumbed down." The only two I can think of that were significantly changed were in the Deku Tree, of which are better in the remake. The ladder puzzle where you shoot the ladder and it falls down got changed to actually incorporate design language seen later into the game, over design language that is never seen again (because you aren't shooting items directly to lower them in the later portions of the game). The giant side-pillar of barbs that you raise up being on a timer didn't really make sense in the original game either, given that you're hardly in the chamber for long enough either way.

I don't see where any parts that posed a challenge got nerfed. Are we talking the Water Temple, which was extremely obtuse for no reason and only hard because the game was bad at telegraphing where you had to go/not built to make you swap items on and off of Link at all times? Or are we talking Combat, because Combat actually got a major upgrade with how enemies are actually aggressive, and fights actually tend to be faster paced akin to Twilight Princess.

As for "hand-holding," I genuinely don't see how this game is more hand-holdy than the original. Where Navi pauses the game to tell you how to solve a puzzle and points out things like switches in the room. If anything, this game holds your hand less because Navi never gives you puzzle hints anymore.

@VoidofLight yes, and with more resources put towards it instead of rehashing a game that’s been available on just about every Nintendo console since the N64 (missing only the GBA and original DS) it would either be released sooner or have more/better content.

« Training the devs » is a convenient narrative, but sometimes they have to say the quiet part out loud and admit that the Switch 2 is going to be roughly 50 percent rehashes and 50 percent new games.

https://www.polygon.com/nintendo-nate-bihldorff-ocarina-of-time-interview/

Shrinkflation will only accelerate, with Nintendo releasing fewer and fewer games every year.

I stand corrected, I guess Morpha spinning its tentacles a little more makes the game worth 85$. Dissing Master Quest while wanting a more straightforward water temple is a bit odd though (it’s common knowledge that the water temple is actually a lot less frustrating in Master Quest).

The hand holding and toned down difficulty really hurt the experience.

Rubbing the solution to a puzzle in your face is really becoming an issue in Nintendo games lately. Metroid Prime 4 did it, Mario & Luigi, and now Zelda. Feels like you’re playing “Kid’s Mode” or something.

No game is perfect, but this one is dang near. The original Ocarina of Time was a masterpiece, and this takes that masterpiece and improves it. If I had any complaint whatsoever, it would be that I wish there were some cool unique rewards for scanning amiibo. But that would be it, and that's such a miniscule thing. I'm just stunned by how good this game is.

I'm going by my playing experience - as per other reviewers here.... but it's a 10. I'm 48. The original literally put me through college and we all know that was a masterpiece.

So what happens when you take a masterpiece, and improve it in every way? Graphics/Sound/Voice Acting/Expanded Cut scenes/Play Control. I'm judging it by the game itself. Just like the original. No master quest expectations - why would I expect that? You play what's in front of you - not what you think it needs. For me, I'm thinking about this game when I'm NOT playing it. That doesn't happen very often. No game is perfect - not even the original but this one is hands down MORE perfect than the original. It's my highest possible recommendation. 10. Period.

#4169. "We are more concerned about the risks of moving too slowly": Epic get more specific about genAI use in Unreal Engine and Fortnite development

Epic Games are, dunno if you've heard, on a bit of a genAI kick at the moment. It's been tough to notice unless you listen very hard. Tim Sweeney's lips have been sealed and no reports have spewed forth.

Sark aside, to this point Epic have had far more provocative soundbites and weird marketing lingo to offer than specific detail about how they're using genAI in different parts of their business.

Responding to questioning from This Week in Videogames, Epic's executive vice president of development Marcus Wassmer's run through some of the exact tools and uses that make up the company's current deployment of the tech.

"There are a number of tools in use but probably the most obvious ones are Claude Code and Codex with their associated AI models," he said "They’re helping across a broad spectrum of development, with some particularly big recent wins being almost the complete elimination of non-deterministic cooking bugs which we’ve been fighting for a decade and an acceleration of work related to compressing shaders which both significantly reduce patch sizes. [Other wins include] a rewrite of a significant portion of the D3D12 rendering layer (which I estimated as needing three to six weeks of work for a single engineer, but the work was actually completed in about one week with a nice win on CPU time and fewer bugs), lots of help in keeping our internal test suites healthy as well as expanding those test suites for more coverage."

Wassmer went on to add that Fortnite's seen the additions of "automatic monitoring of PC stability", "automatic root cause analysis and automatic fix generation", which he claims have sped up the rectifying of long-running issues. He also noted that, engine-wise, Epic have been able to attempt "some larger architectural refactors with AI" than they previously could due to the amount of file changes required.

The dev went on to confirm that the Epic Store launcher preview released the other week isn't the only bit of vibe-coding the company have been up to, with the practice also being used in Unreal Engine development. "Yes, we are vibe-coding things," he said. "That means our engineers are no longer writing the bulk of the code, but they are still guiding the tools to get the architectural result we want. We’re not ‘one-shotting’ the engine; we’re iterating with AI to ship features developers want and keep the engine within the memory, performance, and scalability envelopes."

Wassmer also managed to fit in some justification as to why Epic see no other way forward then shoving a bunch of genAI into their development, largely parroting the typical talking point of 'everyone's going to be doing it soon and we can't possibly be seen to miss out on that gold rush for short-term speediness, baby'. "We are more concerned about the risks of moving too slowly than we are about AI skepticism," is one of the lines he actually said.

To be fair, at least Wassmer and Epic aren't hiding the fact they're embracing this stuff, as much as Timmy Sweens hates the concept of devs having to disclose their genAI use to prospective customers or users. Sometimes the desire of AI bros to shout about their use from the rooftops out of sheer marketing zeal has its positives, eh?

#4168. 11 Bit Studios Signs Deal To Release Three 'Day One' Xbox Game Pass Titles In 2027

We've already heard about many titles coming to Xbox Game Pass in 2027, including the likes of Stranger Than Heaven and Fable in the first couple of months, and now we know that 11 Bit Studios will be joining the lineup next year too.

The publisher (and developer in some cases) behind such games as Frostpunk 2, The Alters and Moonlighter 2 has officially entered into an agreement with Microsoft to release three upcoming games on Xbox Game Pass.

Here's the confirmation, as shared on social media:

The deal unfortunately doesn't mention what the three games will be, but confirms they're from the "publishing portfolio" (so not necessarily developed by them), and are "scheduled for release in 2027".

Plans for 11 Bit Studios are mostly unknown at the moment, but they are confirmed to be working on a new version of Frostpunk called Frostpunk 1886, along with a psychological horror game called Trainwatch and a narrative-driven survival farming simulator known as Crop. Who knows whether any of these will make the cut for Game Pass though.

Let's wait and see! We've had a lot of fun with a whole bunch of 11 Bit Studios titles on Xbox Game Pass over the years, and these three upcoming titles should prove excellent additions to the service in 2027 - whatever they may be.

"It’s hard to put into words what that means to us"

Fraser is the News Editor at Pure Xbox, where he spends his time reporting on the biggest stories in the world of Xbox and beyond.

It's a decent value for those that do but I'd rather just buy the digital rights on a sale for a lot of these games. Stranger Than Heaven will some day be $20 and that's a month of game pass right there. Good they keep signing exclusives but how much has the player base shrunk in the upper tiers I wonder?

@mac_da_man It made no impact on the latest COD not being on there.It's like blaming the poor sales of Wolverine on PS Premium if they had Day One games on there. The fact is it doesn't mean just because it's a day one AAA game that everyone is going to rush out and buy it.

Just like what Matt Piscatella had to say about Gamepass Day One games. Game Pass Ultimate costs $23 a month.Let's not say that Gears was 'free' with Game Pass, ok?Game Pass isn't free. The framing is ludicrous.

And it isn't straight cannibalism if a person paying for Game Pass plays an offered game through the service.Please. Let's be serious people. Or at least try to be.

Not every person who plays a game via a sub service would buy that game were it not included in that service.

Just like that silly math that floated around last year about what Call of Duty "lost" being on GP by multiplying GP players by the full price of the game.

So are you saying that Game Pass makes no difference to the revenue a game brings in, @Schonks? Because it absolutely does, just as @mac_da_man said!

I totally agree with you that not everyone that plays a game on Game Pass would buy the game, however, if even one third of the people that played the game via Game Pass bought the game instead, then Microsoft would be making more money. Game Pass at $23 as opposed to paying $70 (or more for it).

Plus, it needs to be remembered, that if someone plays through E-Day in a couple of weeks, and then plays something else on Game Pass then that is not just a saving on the $70 E-Day, it is also a saving on whatever else they played. Indeed, instead of paying $23 to play one $70 game they could be paying $23 to play two games worth $70 or more.

I accept, as I said above, that not everyone would buy a game that they played on Game Pass. I really do. However, if you look at E-Day itself, 711,000 people bought the Premium Edition Upgrade, and I would contend that if people are willing to spend $30 on that upgrade, they are probably Gears of War fans, meaning that if the game had not been on Game Pass, many more than just a third of them would have bought the game.

Honestly though, I would not be swayed by a corporate suit coming out to defend something that is being criticised because he has to do so to ensure that investors don't get too concerned. We see it all the time, and it does not mean that we should just swallow what they say hook, line and sinker. He's right, people playing E-day on Game Pass are not playing the game for free, but that is nowhere near the same as saying the game would have earned more had it not been on the service.

I think ultimately, we will know by or before April next year (at the end of the fiscal year) whether the day one Game Pass first-party games will continue, and my money is that they will not...

So think about it for a while, it will make sense.

#4167. Honkai: Star Rail Version 4.3 will take us deeper into the World in Canvas and make Mortenax Blade playable

Honkai: Star Rail's next big outing will see the continuation of the Planarcadia story, and it's going to be with us soon.

HoYoverse has today delivered full details on the next major update for Honkai: Star Rail. Version 4.3, dubbed The Lethe Below the Living, will be available for all players on June 1. The upcoming update adds a new chapter to the Planarcadia arc, and introduce a new playable character.

The new narrative chapter will also unveil more about Mortenax Blade, the Trailblazer themselves, and the husk of the Aeon.

Mortenax Blade is the hero of this chapter, and he’s going to step into the World in Canvas. The goal is to - by borrowing the power of Voracity - excise Shuhu from his body and end the curse.

The Trailblazer goes on a trip of their own in Version 4.3, this time to Inkford Hermitage, right on the edge between the World in Canvas and the real world. They’re going to undertake this journey to warn Graphia of the Asat Pramad threat.

In case you hadn’t already guessed, Mortenax Blade is this version’s new playable character. The 5-Star Fire-Type swordsman is on the Path of Nihility. Blade’s Ultimate allows him to enter an enhanced state by deploying a special Bounded Field.

While the field is active, all enemies receive more DMG. Entering this state is also how Blade unlocks his skill, which uses a Sword Formation to deal more damage. This is then used to essentially unlock a second, more powerful Ultimate for him.

The benefits of Mortenax Blade’s kit extend to his teammates, too. Any ally who attacks an enemy with him on the team, they inflict a debuff on them. This also builds up a special Charge that Blade can later use with his Skill.

Version 4.3’s launch arrives alongside the Gift of Tempered Blade event. Through it, you can claim a new Trailblazer Outfit piece for free, but only after getting Mortenax Blade from Warping. The first phase’s rerun will be Yao Guang, and the second phase will bring back both Cyrene and Phainon.

You can also expect the Wispae Amusement Park to arrive within the World in Canvas, which you’ll get to design. You can plan where the rides will go, pick the different themes, set visitor routes and more.

Starward Mode is another new addition, which can be found in Memory of Chaos, Pure Fiction, and Apocalyptic Shadow. Starward will see you take on three different stages, which you’ll need three teams for. Clearing each challenge with full stars will reward you 100 Stellar Jades extra per chase.

There’s more coming down the line, too. A new Fate/Stay Night [Unlimited Blade Works] collaboration will arrive in a content up this summer. The event will give players a chance to earn Gilgamesh or Archer for free by logging in.

#4166. Company of Heroes 3's Operation Torch DLC ships off to North Africa in November, for new missions based around the Allied landings

Atten-shun! Company Of Heroes 3's got new single-player missions inbound via a DLC set during the Allies' 1942 invasion of North Africa. You'll take charge of American forces through a campaign steeped in second world war history that's designed to test your tactical nous and ability to upgrade fighting units to come out on top.It's out on November 25th.

As is made rather obvious by its name, the DLC depicts Operation Torch, which saw the Brits and yanks work together to invade Vichy France-controlled Algeria and Morocco. There's a "dramatic campaign arc that spans the opening invasion, the defeat at Kasserine, and the final assault on Hill 609", no doubt with copious mentions of names like Eisenhower and Patton across its 15 missions.

You'll don the boots of three American soldiers who're either in command or in the thick of the action on the battlefield, with devs Relic noting that their "perspectives reflect the hardships, losses, responsibilities, and lessons learned as they are forged into the fighting force that will liberate Europe".

In between the likes of urban tank battles and stealth ops, you'll pick upgrades earned through completing objectives, ensuring your troops fight in the manner that best suits your preferred tactical slant. For example, I assume you'll be able to go all-in on artillery if all you're after is some big booms that look impressive, but might prove useless if the enemy are safely tucked away in deep cover waving their middle fingers at your boys.

"Company Of Heroes 3 is a rip-roaring return to form and then some for Relic's much loved RTS, and its stirring orchestral score will have you beating your chest and yelling hoo-rah like only the best toy soldier fantasies can," former RPS commander-in-chief Katharine wrote of COH 3 on release in 2023. "If Relic can iron out some of those lingering campaign niggles, this could easily be an all-timer for WWII strategy buffs."

More recently, current boss Julian gave roguelite spin-off Company of Heroes 3: Final Stand a go, coming out with the impression that it's a shakeup which succeded in increasing his appreciation for the series.

#4165. Cyberpunk trading sim Probably Stolen is about running a kiosk in a space station full of gangs, megacorps, and secret rogue cyborgs

I will have you know this is an original Malorian Arms 3516

I have so far not been shivved, shanked, brain fried, hazed, wasted, ironed, short-circed, flat-lined or even complained at in Probably Stolen - Cyberpunk Shopkeeper Sim, but I'm sure it's just a matter of time.

In this neuromantic kiosk game from Questing Goose Studio, you're a new store owner aboard a backwater space station. Each day, you roll up the shutter and do business with a procession of shady types, ranging from janitors with unappetising beards to sexy cowled folk with Main Character tattoos. The basics are simple enough, for all the overwhelmingly menu-led presentation: buy what you can afford, according to your instinct for the wider market, sell what you can fit into the customer's budget. But things quickly get complicated.

You've got to watch out for wanted criminals, checking them against mugshots and possibly, reporting them to security. You've got to think about how your transactions shape the opinions of various factions, from revolutionaries through corpo bosses to the mob. You've got to run a magnifying glass over robot hands and cigarette packets, identifying vintage pieces and counterfeits. You've got to head out at night to scrounge stock from the dumps, preferably without getting shivved, shanked, etcetera. You've got to pay the electricity bill. You've got to shoot rogue androids in the CPU.

I've only peeked timidly over the counter of Probably Stolen, which I would cautiously characterise as Papers, Please with a lot more wheeling and dealing, but it feels like there's some decent substance here. I'm particularly intrigued by the idea of diversifying my operations beyond bog-standard checkout work.

"Start as a gunsmith, chemist, water merchant, fence, farmer, or from absolute rock bottom," the Steam page growls. "Every product line has its own profit curve and its own way of ruining you, weapons bring inspections, chemicals bring addiction, water brings liability, contraband brings raids. Some trades need heavy machinery and permits, others just a good hiding spot and a straight face. The better the margins, the worse the consequences when something goes wrong. You’re not choosing a theme for your shop, you’re choosing which kind of trouble you’re willing to monetize."

Oof! I'll use that closing line next time I interview a producer about season passes. Maybe I'll use it next time I have to pick a wallpaper pattern for my flat.

As cyberpunk fictions go, this does seem very comfortable. Your store has a cassette player with a selection of synthy music - I turned it off after 30 seconds, because the tunes were so gratingly generic. Dare I say it, cyberpunk is a "cosy" genre these days, but perhaps I just need to trade up to some classier earworms.

I also don't think much of Probably Stolen's writing, which seems clipped and flavourless, but it's getting the job done, and besides, I'm very early on in my career as a skanky pawnshop operator. I haven't even sold any toilet roll yet, and that feels like the real rite of passage. People who prefer their Netrunner 7-Elevens all 3D and hung with beautiful, beautiful birdcages might prefer the dives you get in No Law, which Julian saw recently.

#4164. Monopoly Go x The Simpsons crossover is almost here

After a long wait and exhaustive leaks, the highly-anticipated Simpsons event will finally arrive in Monopoly Go very soon, alongside new content.

Monopoly Go players have been looking forward to a major crossover event for what felt like months, and though most of the details ended up leaking, nothing actually beats official information.

The world of The Simpsons has officially arrived in Monopoly Go, and there's a whole lot for players to dive into. The show's creative team even produced a new animated short, featuring Mr. Monopoly, and Mr. Burns.

Available June 3 through July 29, the new event allows Monopoly Go players to jump in the world of The Simpsons. You'll be able to build, and explore all around multiple iconic locations from the show.

Along the way, you'll run into Simpsons characters like Homer, Marge, Bart, Lisa, and of course, Mr. Burns. Developer Scopely teamed up with the show's creative team to create many references, and Easter Eggs for you to discover. You'll find some of those on chance cards, but most of the world has been changed to be part of The Simpsons, including getting to bribe Chief Wiggum to escape jail.

The developer promises a deeply connected world with Simpsons narratives and characters that alter seasonal maps, and offer unique sticker sets and animated sequences to dive in. Incidentally, this is The Simpsons' first appearance in a mobile-exclusive game in 13 years.

Here's a breakdown of everything you can expect, straight from Scopely:

Episodes: Narrative-driven encounters that create stories inspired by The Simpsons. Episodes play out across seasonal boards, sticker sets, and minigames, all capped off with an animated short.

Sticker sets: Every Episode comes with its own limited-time sticker set, taking cues from the latest Simpsons story. Collectible artwork, character journeys and other rewards are yours to claim for the duration of each Episode.

The Simpsons Run: Every two weeks, a new Springfield character will take over the Free Parking tile, kicking off character-driven runs.

Simpsons-themed Shutdowns and Heists: Monopoly Go's shutdowns and heists get a Simpsons makeover, with Springfield-inspired chaos and disasters.

Bribe Wiggum: This changes Go to Jail to allow players to bribe Chief Wiggum, giving you a chance to earn a bigger reward, but not without introducing an element of unpredictability.

Simpsons chance cards: The chance card collection grows with over 50 Simpsons-themed cards full of memes, references and one-liners from the show.

If you're excited to jump in tomorrow, be sure to check out these Free Monopoly Go Dice Links before you dive into the new content.

Collecting Moji's House Key in Phantom Blade Zero is quite easy as it's right at the end of a path, in the middle of the Mandate Encampment, making it near enough impossible to miss. Moji's House Key is found upstream just after defeating the Chief Disciple of the Seven-Stars Formation boss. Since defeating this boss is also how you get the Phantom Blade Zero Training Grounds Key, the route to Moji's House Key is exactly the same, so here's where you go:

You at least get Remnant Dust for each page, and the final one is a map that highlights the mountain path on the northeastern side of Lake Meigu. Follow the directions of Moji's map and you can finally complete the Phantom Blade Zero Whence The Weeping quest, as well as several others.

#4161. GTA 6 has a smell reaction system, which immediately joins Red Dead Redemption 2's dynamically shrinking horse balls on Rockstar's list of immersive symbols of excess

Florida of course being full of smelly smells that smell...smelly

Any reminder of Red Dead Redemption 2's temperature sensitive horse testicles brings a smile to my face. In truth, I can't say I've ever zoomed in close enough to properly take in the spectacle of Arthur Morgan's mount having its nuts dynamically expand and contract based on whether he's riding through snowy mountains or across baking plains, but I do always get a kick out of knowing such a thing's happening as I play. To this point, the horse balls have been the most infamous or meme-worthy example of Rockstar's obsession with going all-in on realistic detail to an arguably unnecessary degree, one that borders on overindulgence which players could conceivably never notice if they weren't expressly told about it.

That philosophy's gone nowhere, so GTA 6 was always going to have a feature that'd become as much of a metaphor for excess as those beloved balls. It may well be the smell reaction system revealed in Edge's long read on the game.

According to this latest rundown of things in GTA 6 and how they were made, Rockstar devs at one point had to make a character react to a not nice smell for a specific bit of "explorable content" stuffed into the game. Cool. One person scrunching their face up to show things are getting stinky in one minigame or mission. Leave it at that.

They reportedly did not leave it at that, later going back to flesh out this one smell reaction into a broader system which other locations to inspire various degrees of face-scrunching by protagonists Lucia and Jason. Cue, in the demo of the game in action which Rockstar gave Edge, Jason walking into a house and starting to act like someone who's just walked into a shower-averse teenager's bedroom during a heatwave despite that not having been set up as part of a deliberately crafted encounter. It's horse ball-esque dynamic systems playing off each other, and voila, a man going eewwwwwwwwwwwww.

Would GTA 6 be any worse off if, as in previous entries, you weren't being shown as expressly which places the crim whose boots you're sharing finds a bit too pongy for their liking? Almost certainly not, but hey, when you've decided your business is taking the detail to levels other games could only dream of having the budget for, getting to the point where you're adding a fiftieth layer of icing to a cake so packed to the gills with different tastes and flourishes that your guests will struggle to appreciate or even notice them all unless you painstakingly point out each one is sort of inevitable.

Another layer of gold wrap on the Bugatti, another brick made of diamonds in a wall projected to be the most lucrative of all time, another farty stench in a room already drowning in foul aromas. It's beautiful in the perverse sort of way that I imagine the Palace of Versailles was to anyone who wandered its gilded halls just prior to the French revolution. To be clear, this isn't any sort of slight on the devs who'll no doubt have worked hard to bring this system and others in GTA 6 to life, a number of whom have a recoginition vote on their unionisation efforts coming up next month.

From a player perspective, one can only hope that by the time GTA 6 hits PC, the RAM crisis has led hardware makers to invest heavily in smellivision tech, so that players around the world can drink in the guffs causing their butt naked on-screen analogue's eyes to water or revel in the stink caused by hitting someone with a bag of dog shit. Forget AI bollocks, this is the future, I scream as I retch into a toilet bowl while some funky tunes from Justice play in the background.

#4160. Hideo Kojima Is 'Inventing A New Medium' - Bill Skarsgård Shares Why Starring In Xbox's PHYSINT Is A 'Big Deal'

"I think Kojima is a pioneer, and keeps going out to untrodden waters"

Hideo Kojima always brings a certain sense of mystery and allure to his work, as is currently the case with the OD KNOCK and PHYSINT projects. For quite some time, speculation over who would star in the latter threw all sorts of crazy names into the mixer, before Kojima revealed that Pennywise and Dune actor Bill Skarsgård had got the job.

Skarsgård recently appeared on the Happy Sad Confused podcast, where he spoke about how working with Hideo Kojima is a "big deal" for him. He also admitted that he grew up playing all the Metal Gear Solid games and is a big fan of Kojima's process.

"I played every single one [Metal Gear Solid], at least the ones on platform. So, I was very enamoured by him and the sort of the mythology or the universes that he creates, but also the sort of mystique and allure about him as well."

As the actor continued to praise the Metal Gear creator, Skarsgård seemed to specifically be impressed by Kojima's fluent knowledge of filmmaking despite being a video game developer. He even recalled a moment where he asked Kojima if he would ever make a film:

"[Kojima] is an auteur, but he's a video game auteur. He's fluent in filmmaking, in film, and in cinema. I remember at one point, way back 20 years ago, there was talk about doing a Metal Gear Solid movie, and, is gonna Hideo gonna direct it? I asked him, 'would you ever do a film?' and he's like 'no'. At this point, what he's doing is inventing a new medium."

Skarsgård touched briefly on his performance capture in PHYSINT and suggested he's working on eight hours of narrative storytelling.

"What we're gonna do is eight hours worth of narrative, right? But it's also an entire universe that you play, so it truly is quite literally world building. But now with technology, we're getting closer and closer to something that's photorealistic, but it's also interactive when you play it. I think he's a pioneer, and keeps going out to untrodden waters."

PHYSINT is a return to tactical espionage for Kojima since departing Konami and Metal Gear Solid in 2015. We're very excited to see what he's been cooking up with Bill and the rest of the cast when we eventually learn more. Xbox has also remained fairly quiet on how PHYSINT fits into Microsoft's exclusivity plans.

#4159. Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 intro cinematic is "not intended to reference or trivialise" real-world South Korean crowd crush, Activision say amid reported backlash

Update: Activision reportedly confirm footage will be removed in November Modern Warfare 4 update

Update: The BBC report that Activision have issued a statement apologising to the victims of the Itaewon crowd crush and confirmed that the news footage from the disaster in Modern Warfare 4's intro cinematic will be removed. An update coming to the shooter on November 12th will do the deed.

The 10.29 Itaewon Disaster Bereaved Families Association have welcomed Activision's decision to pull the footage, according to the BBC, but also said they hadn't received a direct apology from the Call of Duty publishers.

The intro cinematic of Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4, this year's Activision mil-shooter, has reportedly caused controversy in South Korea due to the use of some real world news footage from a 2022 crowd crush in Seoul's Itaewon district which killed around 150 people. Activision have now issued a response to the situation, in which they state the intro is "not intended to reference or trivialise the Itaewon disaster or any other real-world tragedy".

Korean site SBS News have reported on the backlash Modern Warfare 4's opening cinematic has caused in the country. Their story - which it's worth noting has been translated into English by AI, and thus is acknowledged as potentially containing errors - claimed that the shooter's intro features three seconds of real-world broadcast footage showing a emergency workers performing CPR on a collapsed person during the Itaewon crowd crush's aftermath.

The crush saw a crowd of people become trapped in a narrow alleyway during Halloween weekend celebrations in the South Korean capital, with between 150 and 160 people dying as a result of becoming so tightly packed together that some couldn't breathe. According to the report, groups and bodies in Korea including an association representing families who suffered bereavements in the crush have called for Activision to remove the footage from Modern Warfare 4's intro.

Approached for comment by RPS, Activision issued the following statement on the situation:

Modern Warfare 4's campaign is built around a North Korean invasion of South Korea.

#4158. Rumour: Data Found In Zelda: Ocarina Of Time May Hint At Master Quest DLC

One of our main bugbears with Zelda: Ocarina of Time on Switch 2 – as incredible as it is – is that it's overall quite a breezy experience for those already familiar with the original or 3DS release.

As such, we thought it might beneficial if Nintendo were to include a more difficult mode, whether it be a simple Hero Mode in which enemies deal more damage, or perhaps even a port of the reworked Master Quest mode from the GameCube and 3DS.

Our prayers may (emphasis on the 'may') soon be answered, as a post from MrCheeze on BlueSky reveals that data found in Ocarina of Time may be hinting at some sort of Master Quest content. You'll see in the image below that many of the lines of data include 'MQ' next to the title 'DodongoCavern'.

MrCheeze has also provided more information in a follow-up post, stating "Couple strings in the exefs as well giving some context (HasMQ, IsMQModeExist, NewGameMQ, ReleaseMQ)".

So does this mean Master Quest is on the way? Potentially. We're not quite ready to put money on it, but it would certainly make sense for Nintendo to include it as part of a DLC expansion, whether free or paid.

Almost all first-party Nintendo games these days include some sort of post-launch DLC, so we've no reason to believe Ocarina of Time would be any different. As ever, though, do take all of this with a pinch of salt.

In a recent interview with IGN, producer Eiji Aonuma stated " I don't think that we would announce anything specific at this time" when asked whether Master Quest was considered for the Switch 2 remake.

#4157. Can the SideWinder Game Pad, Microsoft's first game controller, work on modern PCs? I bought three of them to find out

The past and fiddly present of the Xbox controller's ancestor

1996 gave us two incredible gifts. The first was me. The second, arguably more impactful on the course of human civilisation, was the Microsoft SideWinder Game Pad 1.0.

Chances are you might not have heard of the SideWinder brand. Launched in 1995 with the 3D Pro and Standard joysticks, the hardware family would eventually comprise gamepads, racing wheels, a game voice device to talk with friends and vocally control your game, and a massive mouse with more buttons than my nana’s vest. A genuinely cool collection of peripherals.

However, and perhaps prophetic of how they would eventually set about dismantling a gaming industry they had helped built, Microsoft shuttered the SideWinder brand in 2003, supposedly due to poor sales. An especially funny comment, in hindsight, came from Microsoft Canada’s then marketing manager, Kim McWhinnie:

"While SideWinder devices are very popular, the majority of PC games today are built for a mouse and keyboard interface.”

Well before the yacht-printing success of the Steam Deck and handheld PC gaming, a significant chunk of PC players have long preferred the feel and functionality of a controller. Although the SideWinder name enjoyed a brief resurrection in 2007 with the release of the SideWinder Mouse, and later the SideWinder X6 and X4 keyboards, the gamepad side of the brand would never again see another product, with Microsoft instead opting for PC-compatible versions of their Xbox controllers.

Which bring us to 2026. While making my weekly car boot excursion, the fates conspired to bring me and the SideWinder Game Pad 1.0 together, in the form of a nice old lady asking for 2 euros. Bonafide hardware history, for that little cash? I was sold, and determined to see how a controller from the 90s might stand up to PCs and games of the 21st century.

Sadly, the initial feel of the controller isn’t great. The shell is cut from cheap plastic that sits awkwardly in my hands. Rather than a thumbstick, the controller boasts this odd circular D-Pad that allows for eight directional movement, though the diagonals are notably harder to press. The triggers give a nice clicking sound, but they feel far too thin to enjoy pushing down. The buttons are fine, though the press is much too soft for my thumb-tastes.

The controller does appear to have built with the idea of 'serious gaming' in mind. For instance, the pad comes bundled with software allowing for the creation of macros that can then be deployed at the push of the big M on the controller. Other interesting details include the early design choices that would eventually be mimicked on the first Xbox controller, the "Duke". The omni-directional D-Pad and the triple button rows make their debut here, though the size of the controller is much more in line with the later "Controller S" model, which shed much of the Duke’s girth.

The SideWinder also came with a rather neat 'pass through' port, allowing owners to connect additional SideWinder controllers through the initial controller, daisy chaining up to a total of four. Sadly, I lacked the friends necessary to examine this aspect, so you’ll have to make do with the purely imaginary scenario of securing victory by pulling on your controller hard enough to yank everyone else’s to the ground. Which, if nothing else, shows Microsoft really understood their target audience.

There's no denying the power of old controllers to provoke fond memories in the handler, nor their continued popularity in the modern day - as evident in Nintendo's production of imitation Gamecube and NES pads for the Switch 2. With growing preferences for emulation in the face of bankrupting retro game prices, many either go for custom controllers with modern functionality, or original peripherals connected via adapters, in order to preserve as much of the original experience as possible. But can the same be said for the SideWinder?

While I tracked down an old TV ad for the controller, my trawling of numerous old gaming magazines was less fruitful. I did come across a glowing review from the November 1996 issue of PC Zone by Dave Mathelson, praising the "two clever underneath buttons" (triggers were, indeed, a novelty at the time) and describing the handles as "horns" and the general design, more concerning, as "sexy". The verdict was almost entirely positive, praising both the feel and the ability to create custom control schemes for each of your games. Yet, I feel this line perhaps betrays the controller's struggles:

"While there are plenty of pads now available for the PC, the number of joysticks on the market didn't stop Microsoft from releasing one..."

As much as I find the SideWinder interesting, I'd argue it's more generic-looking than sexy. The late 90s/early 00s gave us attitude, explosions, and impractical designs you could only get by locking up a bunch of coked-up mandrills with CAD modelling software. An era ruled by the SpaceOrb 360 and the Fragmaster, the kind of creations birthed by an out-of-touch executive demanding kung-fu grip. Even Microsoft's own SideWinder Strategic Commander, an early attempt at an RTS mouse, had that strangeness sauce.

By comparison, the SideWinder Game Pad cuts a very subtle figure. There’s a seriousness to it. Still playful, as we are dealing with gaming. The nerd equivalent of dressing up in a new suit but leaving the top button undone. It feels like they were going for something more professional. The macro feature and the ability to customise your controller scheme for each game accentuate this point further, while also showcasing a design ethos Microsoft have long since abandoned: trusting consumers with the product you sold them.

Yet this also means it doesn’t stand out. I think Microsoft must have realised this at some point, as later additions to the SideWinder brand are more distinct, both visually and functionally. The Force Feedback Pro went on to sell over a million units, but the Game Pad hardly gets a mention in the news archives. For every Reddit post or TikTok short or LGR Review on weird and wonderful tech, the bland 1.0 is memory-holed even deeper.

Then, of course, there’s one other serious issue that keeps the SideWinder buried in the cable bin of yesterday: modern compatability.

As you can imagine, these things aren’t exactly easy to get working on a present-day PC.

My desktop, despite being a little dated itself, lacked the necessary connections to test the SideWinder. My motherboard still boasts old-school PS2 connectors for keyboard and mouse, but couldn’t spare a thought for more specialised retro gear. Granted, it’s not hard to see why. The controller (and a lot of the tech from the era) makes use of a 15-pin game port connector, appearing first on dedicated PCI cards, then later sound cards and eventually motherboards. These would eventually be phased out as USB became the go-to connector for personal computers, and while game port-to-USB adapters do exist, and even come bundled with later SideWinder products, procuring one today is surprisingly difficult.

So I went for the next best thing: a sound card from the 90s. A Creative Sound Blaster Live, torn from some ancient machine to grace me with the soft beauty of 16-bit audio and the game port’s connective tissue. I then quickly discovered that the card wasn’t compatible with my motherboard. Growing desperate as I battled both a looming deadline and my partner’s concern at the growing horde of retro tech, I managed to find someone selling two more SideWinders AND the game port-to-USB adapter. I snapped them up, plugged the adapter into my system, aaaaaand...

Nothing. The computer just couldn’t find it.

I’m saddened to admit I still attempted to get the blasted thing working long after this, eventually culminating in injuring myself while attempting to plant the sound card in an older machine. Taking this as a sign from the tech gods that I was not truly worthy of enjoying this artifact, I instead settled for a slightly newer (albeit still ancient) SideWinder Plug and Play. This came with USB out of the box, at the cost of fewer buttons and even less individuality, but I felt it would serve to at least give you some idea of how a SideWinder controller plays. Rest assured that if you think this damages the integrity of this retrospective, there is no one more ashamed than myself.

Prior to writing the article, I had a chat with my dad regarding the SideWinder Game Pad. He couldn’t stop gushing about it, saying how it was one of his favourite controllers back in the day. Unlike with Father Christmas, it appears my dad was telling the truth. The Plug and Play was genuinely fun to use, though perhaps not for the reasons my dad would expect.

I immediately fired up a multiplayer lobby of Titanfall 2, an FPS defined by its intricate movement systems, and proceeded to patiently stroll down the city streets, gaze locked forward. I could neither sprint nor turn the camera. In addition, incomplete control mapping also meant I couldn’t even shoot. I nearly fell out of my chair laughing as I was absolutely and immediately demolished.

I gave the original, 1993 Doom a whirl next, though again faced the issue of needing to dual wield with my PC mouse to rotate the camera for effective demon slaying. I ended up crab-walking into rooms, running back out, and letting the enemies funnel into my view. So somewhat more successful here.

Continuing my testing through retro and modern alike, I unleashed eco justice with Cloud in the original Final Fantasy VII, went bust in a round of Balatro, and tended to my farm in Stardew Valley. The SideWinder held up in all of them. I also gave some upcoming indie demos a whirl, successfully battling a demonic incursion in Entropy but tragically getting torn apart by bugs in The Last Exterminator.

Overall, so long as your game doesn’t require too many inputs (and also ideally takes place entirely within a straight hallway), the controller works great. My verdict? Ideal for Deep Space Corridor.

I'm sure that the SideWinder Game Pad 1.0 can be made to work with modern systems. Given enough time and a few more blows to my bank account, I could either fit my computer with the correct hardware, or hack together a game port adapter with an Arduino board.

I don’t intend to give up, but it’s also a pain point that’s going to be too much for a lot of people. Tech continues to hurtle forward, abandoning anything deemed inefficient for the world of tomorrow, with little care for ensuring compatabiltiy with the successes of yesterday. Sony already showed as much with their promise/threat to ditch physical games media. Do you think Microsoft are going to care about a controller that Asha Sharma has probably never heard of, much less used?

The truth of the matter is that, as foundational as the tech is, the SideWinder Game Pad was just an early casualty in an arms race that has slowly stripped uniqueness, choice, and especially this past year, affordability from players. Give it another decade, and if the tech overlords have their way, we’ll likely be renting our machines, streaming our games, and paying per hour for the privilege of using a controller.

Now, if you’ll excuse me, I’m going to enjoy my four SideWinders while I still can.
