#4124. Guide: Best Zelda Games Of All Time

Where does the Ocarina of Time remake rank?

You probably haven't heard, but there's a new Zelda game out. Launched last week, in fact.

Oh, you have? Well then, you may be wondering where it ranks with all the other Zeldas - and indeed with the other Ocarinas of Time. Wonder no more; we asked Nintendo Life readers for their verdict, and you can see the result below. Enjoy!

Review The Legend Of Zelda: Ocarina Of Time (Switch 2) - A Stunning Remake, But Not Quite Definitive

What are the best Zelda games? Following decades of adventures across Nintendo consoles, ranking The Legend of Zelda series is one hell of an undertaking. Most stand among the very best games on their respective consoles, so assembling a ranked Zelda list is no small task.

We've compiled this list of the best Zelda games to help you sort the Hyrules from the Lorules. It includes every mainline game, remasters and remakes, and significant spin-offs.

So, let's grab the Master Sword and our Hylian Shield and head out on an adventure. Here is the Legend of Zelda series ranked from worst to best.

On this page: Best Zelda Games Of All Time

An introduction to the little-used plastic Wii Zapper peripheral, Link's Crossbow Training is a little nine-level high-score shooting game which uses various assets and areas from Twilight Princess as Link attempts to improve his crossbow skills using the Wii Remote's pointer functionality.

It's not unenjoyable, and you can pick the disc up for next to nothing these days. While there are sections where you can control Link in a first/third-person perspective, it should not be confused with a fully-fledged Zelda game in any way, shape or form. It is, however, a fun little aside in the Legend of Zelda-verse.

One of several multiplayer-focued Zeldas, Tri Force Heroes, while not a bad game, pales in comparison to other series entries (and the Four Swords games in particular).

You play as Blue, Green, and Red Link, and work together to battle bosses, solve puzzles, and gather loot. The big new feature was the Totem mechanic, which enabled you to stack the three Links on top of each other, although it just wasn't enough to elevate this entry.

Tri Force Heroes still exudes the charm of the franchise and throws in some delightful features all of its own. Outfits are a high point, as are the presentation and soundtrack, and there are moments of wonder when level design and teamwork come together in harmony.

However, uneven stage design, poor communication options, and a single-player experience that feels like an afterthought put this one at the bottom of the illustrious series' Totem pole.

A radical departure from the original and arguably the most difficult game in the series, Zelda II has enjoyed something of a reappraisal in recent, post-Dark Souls years.

In a series that, in the past, risked becoming by-the-numbers by slavishly sticking to a formula, this first sequel was anything but a repetition. A deeper combat system with RPG levelling elements and side-on platforming villages and dungeons made this a very different take on the Zelda template.

You could argue that too much of its sense of adventure and 'wonder' is lost to frustration, but no more so than in other challenging 8-bit games. If you find the challenge too much to bear, the rewind function in the Nintendo Switch Online version comes in useful. Regardless, if you've bounced off The Adventure of Link in the past, we'd urge you to give it a second look.

The first Four Swords experience — originally an 'add-on' mode included as part of the GBA port of Link to the Past — was multiplayer-only until an enhanced port added a single-player mode and was made available on DSiWare for free for a limited time in 2011 (and later very briefly on 3DS in 2014).

It enabled up to four friends to battle through Hyrule together as four Links in differently coloured garb and is very good, too. If you can find it.

Cadence of Hyrule: Crypt of the NecroDancer Featuring The Legend of Zelda *breathe* is an excellent game, but is it a Zelda game? Short answer: Absolutely.

Long answer: Brace Yourself Games didn't simply swap out Crypt of the NecroDancer's sprites with Link and Zelda. This musical, roguelite take on Hyrule delivers everything you'd expect: the exploration, discovery, wonder, items, dungeons, and — most of all — music, all shot through with a rhythm-based gameplay twist that takes a while to get used to but is immensely satisfying once mastered.

This would be a great Zelda game if you've played all the others to death; it's the most replayable entry, with each new run juggling the landscape and layout of the kingdom (cleverly playing with the notion of Hyrule's ever-changing geography throughout the series), meaning no playthrough will be quite the same.

It won't click with everyone, and if you're after 80-hour epics, look elsewhere. But there are plenty of those already. Having a smaller Hylian experience that feels uniquely fresh and also completely 'Zelda' is a joy.

Hyrule Warriors represented Dynasty Warriors developer Omega Force's first foray into the Zelda universe, and it was clear from the off that the team had a deep respect for the setting and characters of Hyrule.

This first attempt lacked the polish we'd see in its Switch 'sequel', Hyrule Warriors: Age of Calamity, but there was enough hack-and-slash entertainment on offer to make this a rather enjoyable diversion. The game has since been ported to both 3DS and Switch with extra content and improvements, but the Wii U original remains an entertaining addition to the Zelda stable for action fans.

A collaborative adventure in the Legend of Zelda mould was something many had dreamt of for a long time, and the Four Swords part of the GBA port of A Link to the Past made the jump to the TV screen here in Four Swords Adventures.

There's a single-player game in there, but the real meat of the experience involved four players hooking their own GBA to a GameCube with the requisite link cable and controlling their Link in a screen-hopping adventure long before Nintendo went asymmetric with the Wii U gamepad.

It's a brilliant co-op Zelda game hampered only by the fact that it required so much kit to function.

Feature Zelda: Four Swords Was Probably Great, But Finding Pals To Play With? Talk About A Master Quest

The Legend of Zelda: Phantom Hourglass had everything you would expect from a Zelda game and was a worthy stylus-controlled entry on DS.

Starring 'Toon Link' from The Wind Waker, Phantom Hourglass made great use of the touchscreen and, combined with the layout, structure, and design typical of the Zelda franchise, made this a familiar yet fresh entry.

If you missed Phantom Hourglass, don't listen to the naysayers — this is a wonderful little experience that's still worth hunting down.

The Legend of Zelda: Spirit Tracks suffers from a bad reputation, but if you can get past being tied to a track, it really is an excellent game. Trading sailing the high seas for choo-chooing across the kingdom by rail, you plot a route, set the speed, and clear the path of enemies using the train-mounted cannon.

Spirit Tracks gave Zelda a proper role for once and also famously used the DS's microphone; you could blow into it to use the Whirlwind and Spirit Pipes, among other items. A fun idea in concept, although playing in a noisy environment would interfere with its function.

Tweaking, expanding, and in some ways improving on Phantom Hourglass while throwing in new novelties, with a fabulous soundtrack that stands alongside the best of the series, we think it's time to reevaluate this entry in the storied franchise. C'mon, ride the train.

A hack-and-slash take on the Zelda universe originally released on the Wii U before receiving a 'Legends' 3DS port and arriving on Switch in 2018, Hyrule Warriors: Definitive Edition — like many a Musou — is a great time-sink if you fancy giving the grey matter a rest and whooping the behinds of hundreds of moblins at once.

There are dozens — if not hundreds — of hours of content here, all crammed with affectionate nods to the wider series, with familiar characters and the first (and hopefully not last) appearance of Linkle, a girl who believes she is the reincarnation of the series' hero.

Though bloated in places, Hyrule Warriors balances the Zelda and Dynasty Warriors elements well. Group all of that with stellar presentation and impressive portable gameplay, and Omega Force and Team Ninja did an excellent job of doing something new (and weird) with a classic Nintendo property.

Hyrule Warriors: Age of Imprisonment is a stunning slice of action, and perhaps our favourite musou game so far. Lessons have been learned from both Hyrule Warriors and Age of Calamity, resulting in a game that balances big-time story with top-notch combat that's got proper depth to it.

With Zonai devices to play with, a cracking roster, tons of sexy Sync Strikes to pull off, and a ludicrously slick recreation of early Hyrule to set about kicking ass in, this is dream time for hack-and-slash fans and Zelda enthusiasts alike.

Yes, map layouts are still a bit bland, and co-op mode is 30fps, but everything else here combines to make for the best entry in this spin-off franchise to date.

If you're looking for a straightforward Zelda adventure, this battle-heavy quest is about as straightforward as it gets. Oracle of Seasons put combat centre stage but adds in enough originality to keep it from feeling monotonous.

Developed by Capcom subsidiary Flagship and helmed by Hidemaro Fujibayashi, director of several later games including Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom, Seasons was most notable for allowing you to use the Rod of Seasons (shocker!) to shift the world's climate and solve a variety of puzzles, from freezing lakes to growing Deku Flowers. This smart weather-switching system would later be revisited in various other Zelda entries.

There is much incentive to play these games together, and if you're wondering which Oracles game to play first, we'd recommend tackling this one second. Doing so adds in interesting plot twists that enhance the relatively barebones storytelling and enables crucial weapon upgrades that help against the challenging end boss.

It may not be as engrossing as Ages, but Seasons still offers up an old-school adventure that will feel fondly familiar to long-time franchise fans.

Hyrule Warriors: Age of Calamity uses the Dynasty Warriors format, but borrows a layer of Breath of the Wild's polished presentation and story, which elevates it in our eyes.

Boasting a large cast of familiar characters — each with their own movesets and weapons — it gives you the chance to fight the Calamity 100 years before the events of BOTW. Performance could be better in some parts (dramatically better on occasion), but frame rate drops didn't affect our enjoyment of this Hylian hack-and-slasher.

This would be a good option for people who have exhausted BOTW and TOTK but still want to spend quality time in that world. Teaming up with the Four Champions is a treat, and while Age of Calamity is obviously riding on Breath of the Wild's coattails, we enjoyed our time with this quasi-prequel adventure.

Oracle of Ages manages to feel both new and familiar at the same time. Link wields the Harp of Ages, which you could use to travel through time.

Now, he may have already done some time-travelling with his ocarina, but in Oracle of Season's companion piece, it becomes the central aspect of gameplay, primarily used to solve puzzles, by moving a stone in the past to redirect the flow of water in the future, for example, or planting seeds that will grow into trees and vines.

This makes for a puzzle-heavy adventure, one that's enhanced by nuanced, colourful characters, interesting items, and a plot much unlike those previously seen in the franchise.

While many beloved Zelda tropes remain, the game still takes plenty of chances, many of which really pay off. It may have been built on Link's Awakening's engine, but Ages feels like its own game.

What is there left to say about The Legend of Zelda?

The game that started it all holds up well, although be prepared to explore and really work for the answers to puzzles here. A modern game would never ask you to try setting random bushes alight to reveal a hidden passageway without signalling it with a huge neon 'SECRET HERE!' sign. The Legend of Zelda trusted the player and had faith in its own strengths enough to let you miss things.

It was a very unique prospect back in 1987, offering an unparalleled sense of adventure, clever combat mechanics, and a world ripe for exploration. Decades later, developers of titles big and small are still borrowing from it.

A landmark game that still feels fresh. Definitely worth revisiting, although if you've never played the series, we wouldn't recommend playing this one first.

This wonderful version of Link to the Past gave a new generation the chance to catch up with a classic a decade after its SNES debut.

Minor tweaks came along in its transition to the handheld's smaller screen. Link was a lot noisier on GBA thanks to the added voice samples, though fan opinion is divided.

An addition that was universally welcomed, however, was the bundled Four Swords multiplayer quest. Assuming you had friends with GBAs and copies of the game, up to four players could link up for a multiplayer-only Zelda adventure to take on the evil mage Vaati.

Yes, The Legend of Zelda: A Link to the Past and Four Swords is quite the package. Whether this or the SNES classic can be classed as the 'definitive' version is up for debate — we personally love the screen real estate of the TV version — but the GBA port is an excellent way to experience Link's greatest 2D adventure.

The Legend of Zelda: Skyward Sword HD introduced a raft of technical improvements and quality-of-life updates that revitalised the Wii game.

The alternate button control scheme totally worked if you still couldn't get on with the motion controls, the graphics got a sensitively handled HD overhaul, and a once-bothersome sidekick was streamlined into something altogether more useful.

Yes, the locking off of instant travel behind the official amiibo was a misstep, but beyond that issue, this was a great remaster of Zelda game that splits opinion.

With the titular princess taking a starring role in her namesake series for the first time, The Legend of Zelda: Echoes of Wisdom should be the new standard for top-down Zelda going forward.

Rather than abandoning the classic formula, Zelda has shown that the old and the new can come together and produce wonderful results that reward experimentation and reinforce the joy of play.

In our book, this is up there with the best top-down adventures in the series, and we hope we don’t need to wait another 35 years for Zelda to take the lead again.

This beautiful Switch remake of the classic Game Boy entry rebuilt everything from the ground up, and would be a good entry point for younger players into the Zelda series.

On top of the beautiful new art style, it added modern conveniences, a dungeon creator, amiibo support, and lots of little quality-of-life improvements whilst infusing every single square inch of Koholint – every secret passage, Piranha, Pokey, and Pig Warrior – with a level of detail and depth that totally reinvigorated both its timeless story and classic Zelda gameplay for a new generation.

If there's anything holding The Legend of Zelda: Link’s Awakening back, frame drops may distract you from the otherwise absorbing gameplay, especially in docked mode. It's a little thing — and something smoothed out on Switch 2, thankfully — but with the heritage of technical wizardry behind the Game Boy original, imperfect performance is a dent in this game's otherwise glistening armour.

Showcasing the sort of swordplay we'd hoped Twilight Princess would contain, The Legend of Zelda: Skyward Sword was a beautiful entry in the series which dared to try some new ideas, something the franchise desperately needed at the time.

It arguably didn't get everything right, and why Nintendo ditched the beautifully accurate IR pointer in favour of a gyro alternative which required constant re-centering — especially when everyone already had the IR sensor hooked up anyway! — is still a source of confusion for us. We found the MotionPlus swordplay itself excellent, though.

Chronologically, this is the very first game in the Zelda timeline, so it's pretty much required reading for series fans. While it has its naysayers, we look back on our time with Skyward Sword very fondly.

Twilight Princess was simultaneously Zelda's swansong on the GameCube and its introduction on the Wii. It's an excellent action adventure, but not without flaws.

Perhaps its biggest problem is that it did little to shake up the Zelda formula, which was feeling a little tired at this point; it plays a bit too similarly to Ocarina of Time and Wind Waker.

The HD version on Wii U restored the GameCube's orientation — putting Kakariko Village back on the side of the map it should be — while retaining the Wii version's 16:9 aspect ratio and adding a host of minor improvements along with high-definition visuals; TP HD is inarguably the best version of Twilight Princess.

Midna is an all-time great companion, and the game hits some brilliant highs, though perhaps not as consistently as other entries.

The Legend of Zelda: The Minish Cap carried on the trend of giving Link a talking piece of equipment to accompany him on his quest. This time around, it was the Minish Cap — a hat named Ezlo that could shrink Link to microscopic proportions so he can locate the Kinstone fragments and save the tiny Minish people, the Picori.

Another Flagship-developed entry after the company proved itself with the excellent Oracles pair, this was a traditional Zelda adventure that still looks and sounds wonderful, even if it didn't do an awful lot to shake up the formula.

This GBA game introduced a few new items, though — Mole Mitts, Gust Jar, and Cane of Pacci — and allowed Link to learn new sword techniques, as well as gain the ability to fuse elements to his sword. All-in-all, a brilliant bite-sized adventure.

Link's Awakening is a game of contrasts: sadness and joy, bleakness and whimsy, dream and reality, confusion and comfort. Its success lies in its ability to balance these contradictory elements with tight, compelling gameplay and a timeless presentation.

The extra dungeon and other features of this DX version don't add up a huge amount over the original monochromatic release, but it's still a mighty fine game enhanced by the upgraded console's colour palette.

Grezzo's Switch remake might have prettified Koholint Island, but the joyous, quirky characters, melancholy, and beauty of Link's first portable adventure were there right from the very beginning. If you own a Game Boy Color or have any other way to access it — like, say, a Nintendo Switch — this game is essential.

As groundbreaking as it was, the 3D Zelda formula was starting to look a little tired by the mid-2000s, so while Twilight Princess is a very fine game, it lacked the impact of its predecessors.

The additional 'waggle' implemented in the Wii version didn't live up to the ideas of 1:1 swordplay we'd imagined, either. And did the entire world really need mirroring just to make Link right-handed? Still, at the time this was the only way to play the game in 16:9 and it made for a satisfyingly meaty Wii launch title in North America.

Not one for the purists, perhaps — you'll want to track down an expensive copy of the GameCube version for the left-handed, canonical geography of Hyrule (or just play Twilight Princess HD on Wii U).

The Legend of Zelda: Majora's Mask 3D was a magnificent refurbishment. A visual overhaul and streamlined features make this version even more enjoyable than the original N64 release.

Minor flaws seem insignificant against its unique gameplay ideas, its dark and haunting theme, and the ticking clock of its cleverly crafted world. It's strange, perhaps, that a game in which the main premise revolves around repeatedly travelling back in time was so ahead of its time.

In its enhanced form, The Legend of Zelda: Majora's Mask 3D belies its age and stands shoulder-to-shoulder with the very best games on its host system or anywhere else. Simply put, it's a masterpiece that every 3DS owner should play.

The Legend of Zelda: Twilight Princess took the series back to an art style closer to Ocarina of Time, albeit a little earthier and benefiting from the power of the 'Cube.

For many fans, it was the 'realistic' Zelda they'd been pining for after Nintendo took a left turn with The Wind Waker's cel-shading, and although it didn't quite strike all the right notes, it still features some breathtaking dungeons, memorably oddball characters, and a unique atmosphere.

Setting a precedent that Nintendo would later repeat with Breath of the Wild, Twilight Princess straddled generations, bookending the GameCube and launching the Wii with some added waggle and widescreen.

We'd recommend Wii U's HD remaster over this, but if you happen to have a copy of the (now very expensive) GameCube disc to hand, TP still delivers.

When we first heard that the 3DS entry in this venerable series would revisit the world of A Link To The Past, our excitement was tempered with trepidation. The SNES classic is sacred ground and perhaps returning to that Hyrule might sully our memories, or worse, reveal that it wasn’t quite as good as we remember.

Of course, our concern was unwarranted; A Link Between Worlds proved to be spectacular. Like all the best mechanics in the series, its novel wall-painting transformation puzzles were so ingeniously simple that you wondered why the concept hadn’t been hit upon before.

Great use of the system’s 3D feature brought Hyrule to life in a game that rivals the greatest in the series. If – shock! horror! – you’re reading this and you don’t own a 3DS, it’s time to track one down and play one of the very best games in a franchise of winners.

Known colloquially around these parts as Majora's Marmite, the three-day cycle added a constant pressure that turned off many players. However, that cycle is also key to the unique way Majora's Mask focuses on its cast of uncanny characters and soaks the adventure in melancholy and madness.

In fact, 'adventure' isn't quite the right word for this Zelda game. It's more of a Lynchian dreamscape in cartridge form, which isn't for everyone. The excellent 3DS remake is the best way to play these days thanks to some welcome additions for managing your limited time, although the original is conveniently available to play via Nintendo Switch Online.

Wherever you play, the clockwork land of Termina offers something truly unique in the Zelda series.

Oh, and we don't really call it Majora's Marmite.

It would be difficult to argue against The Legend of Zelda: Link's Awakening being the pinnacle of gaming on Game Boy. The developers squeezed an extremely lengthy quest into a miniscule package and pushed just about every facet of the handheld hardware to its limit.

Not only is Link's Awakening not the dumbed-down Zelda adventure many initially feared, but it turned out to be one of the best entries in the series. It laid the foundation for many Zelda mechanics we still see today, introducing flying with Cuccos, trading sequences, playing songs on an ocarina, fishing, and even minibosses.

For such a tiny game, Link's Awakening created enormous shockwaves in the series. If you want to experience the very best that the portable system has to offer, do yourself a favour and get this (or the DX version for Game Boy Color with the extra dungeon that's handily available via Nintendo Switch Online) immediately. As much as we love the Switch remake, we're still in love with the original.

Nintendo breathed new life into The Wind Waker in this HD remaster, taking its timeless art style and giving it a glorious high-def sheen and also making worthwhile improvements to previously flawed aspects of the original. Sailing across the Great Sea, discovering new islands, and exploring exciting dungeons — the designs of which still shine even today – has never been more fun than on Wii U.

Nintendo could have done more in certain areas — there really isn’t anything substantial in the way of new content — and the updated lighting, though lovely in its own right, is not necessarily 'better'; it's heavy on the bloom compared to the sublime original.

Still, The Wind Waker was never in need of a drastic overhaul; this refinement made welcome tweaks that brought it more in line with modern standards. A great game made (for the most part) even greater, then.

As if its library wasn't impressive enough, the 3DS got a wonderful reworking of a game which collects ‘Best Game Of All Time’ awards like beer mats.

It was always going to be good, but Grezzo managed to strike the perfect balance between evoking nostalgia for the N64 original and carefully updating and polishing Ocarina of Time to help it shine in the 21st century. It’s just like you remember, but going back and actually comparing the two reveals that it’s vastly improved and overhauled, from UI to textures to character models and beyond.

We might miss the Stone of Agony's rumble, but all Ocarina of Time 3D's modifications make it a smoother, more player-friendly way to play Ocarina of Time. And everybody should play Ocarina of Time.

These days, the Switch 2 remake is more accessible, but if you have a 3DS, you should really have this, too.

Given the 'Cel-da' controversy that blighted the game at its initial reveal, it's fitting that The Wind Waker has come to be so loved and admired over time.

Where other games of the era struggle under the weight of modern high-definition scrutiny, Toon Link's maiden voyage looks almost as fresh as the day we first set out from Outset Isle to discover what had happened to the Hyrule we once knew.

It's not without flaws (and the HD remake on Wii U addressed many of them) but thinking back, we don't dwell on the repetitive wind conducting, the infamous Triforce shard hunt, or Tingle's sea chart extortion. No, it's the rainbow colours of the tempestuous ocean, the breezy panpipes of Dragon Roost, and the salty self-reflection our voyages brought about that stick in the memory.

Beneath the surface, it's very much a continuation of the 3D Zelda template laid down in Ocarina of Time, but there's undeniable magic in The Wind Waker, and despite its imperfections, it's still one of our very favourites of the series.

It’s impossible to talk about everything that makes The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom so incredible, and making those discoveries yourselves is part of the magic.

It’s also impossible to overstate just how much there is to do in this Hyrule the second time around. Much like its predecessor, this will become your playground for several years, with a little sprinkling of that older Zelda fairy dust mixed into Breath of the Wild’s formula.

Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom is a glorious, triumphant sequel to one of the best video games of all time - absolute unfiltered bliss to lose yourself in for hundreds of hours. And the improved performance of the Nintendo Switch 2 Edition makes it even better.

Review The Legend Of Zelda: Tears Of The Kingdom - Nintendo Switch 2 Edition - A Sublime Sequel, Now Sublimer

The Legend of Zelda: A Link to the Past is one of the best games of all time, and if you haven't experienced it yourself... you probably have through one of the other Zelda games, such was its influence on the series and the entire action-adventure genre.

Link could move diagonally and run thanks to the Pegasus Boots, and he could swipe his sword sideways, allowing for a much wider range when attacking. In fact, A Link to the Past introduced many mainstays of the franchise, including various stalwart items and the idea of parallel worlds.

There's no shortage of 2D and 3D Zeldas to choose from these days, but this 16-bit entry codified the core elements of a 'Zelda game.' It's still got that touch of magic about it many years later. Unmissable.

Ocarina of Time brought The Legend of Zelda into the third dimension as successfully as the plumber made the same leap in Super Mario 64. Yet where Nintendo could throw any playground-style idea into Mario's 64-bit debut, Ocarina had to tell a story and evoke a consistent mood throughout.

Going back these days, the frame rate and cumbersome menus may surprise you, and Hyrule Field feels decidedly polygonal and smaller (more like a field, in fact) compared to the vast kingdom of Hyrule presented in Breath of the Wild.

And yet the pure magic of this game still shines through any ageing systems. This set the template not only for every subsequent Zelda title, but also the majority of action-adventure games for the next three decades. No wonder it's so revered.

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time 3D on 3DS is the more streamlined version, but there are things that Grezzo's excellent remake couldn't quite recapture. Whether it's the Rumble Pak compatibility or the 64-bit mist hanging over Lake Hylia in the early hours, the N64 original still has that special something.

The Switch 2 remake is a stunning modern overhaul, but for some the true Hero of Time will forever wear his polygons proudly.

The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild was a landmark release, both for its franchise and Nintendo. It was the first time that the company truly took on the open-world genre, and by arriving late to the party it embraced the strengths of top-in-class games while also forging its own unique identity.

BOTW was a revolution for the series, but the Legend of Zelda essence is still there — its soul remains, and the end result is captivating. After years of following the same old template, Nintendo bravely took Zelda in a new direction and delivered an absolute triumph which still has us regularly revisiting its iteration of Hyrule. This is the series' best-selling game for a reason.

Its sequel expanded on the open world first presented here, but the excitement of exploring Breath of the Wild's wilderness for the very first is an experience nobody should miss. And the Nintendo Switch 2 Edition polishes out a couple of blemishes with 60fps performance that gives the game new life once more.

Review The Legend Of Zelda: Breath Of The Wild - Nintendo Switch 2 Edition - The Best Way To Play, But 'Zelda Notes' Sucks

This Ocarina of Time remake is a stellar reimagining of the original, one that completely revamps the N64 experience with incredible visuals, modernised gameplay, and vastly improved audio.

Despite some minor blemishes, this is comfortably the most visually stunning work Nintendo has ever put out, and it’s unquestionably the best way to play one of the most seminal games of all time.

The worst thing you can say about it? It is a very safe remake. Despite lots of minor changes, it’s still essentially the same game you’ve likely already played, and veterans of the original or the 3DS remake may find it offers little challenge. The lack of Master Quest stings, too - hopefully it’ll be added in the future.

Still, quibbles aside, this is a glorious, irresistible return for one of the medium's most important works, and something to savour on Switch 2.

There we have it – all the Legend of Zelda games ranked.

Nice work getting through all those adventures. Let's finish with a little post-quest Q&A where we answer the common questions readers have about the Zelda games.

The Zelda series began with The Legend of Zelda, released in February 1986 in Japan, August 1987 in North America, and November 1987 in Europe.

While the game launched for NES overseas, the original Japanese version debuted on the Famicom Disk System, a disc-based add-on console for the Famicom that only launched in Japan.

It wasn't until 1994 that The Legend of Zelda appeared on a Famicom cartridge in Nintendo's homeland.

There are 28 Zelda games in the mainline series, including colour/HD remasters and 3D remakes.

That's counting the Oracles games as separate titles, and includes multiplayer-focused Zeldas such as Four Swords, Four Swords Adventures, and Tri Force Heroes, although there's debate among fans over whether they are truly 'mainline' entries. We'll leave that up to you to decide!

In terms of releases, the newest game in the Zelda series is the Switch 2 exclusive The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake, which launched on 5th Nov 2026.

Both Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom got Nintendo Switch 2 Editions in June 2025 alongside that console's launch, although they are enhanced versions with only minor feature updates and no new content.

The musou spin-off Hyrule Warriors: Age of Imprisonment also launched in November 2025 - while not a mainline entry, its story is canon to TOTK.

The next game in the Zelda series hasn't been announced yet.

Zelda: A Link to the Past for Super NES is a good starting point. We asked Nintendo Life readers and that's what you chose.

LTTP took the outline of the original game and solidified it into an overworld-dungeon template that formed the basis for the entire series. It's available to play on Switch with a Nintendo Switch Online subscription.

Ocarina of Time is another must-play — the first 3D game in the Zelda series, and now with a gorgeous remake available on Switch 2.

Breath of the Wild is considered an excellent first Zelda game.

Talking Point Which Zelda Game Should You Play First?

Where should you start if you're new to The Legend?

Zelda II: The Adventure of Link is commonly said to be the most challenging game in the series.

This NES title is available to play on Switch via Nintendo Switch Online, which also features a handy rewind tool, making getting through Zelda II much more manageable!

Breath of the Wild is currently the best-selling entry in the Zelda series. It has sold 34.28 million copies worldwide as of September 2026.

This is followed by Tears of the Kingdom, which has sold 22.9 million units as of September 2026.

Er, no. Zelda is the princess of Hyrule, the kingdom where much of the series is set. The character who commonly wears a green tunic, hat, and sword is called Link.

Despite the name, Link is the protagonist and player character in the Legend of Zelda series. The Legend of Zelda. Echoes of Wisdom is the sole exception — Zelda herself is the main character in that adventure.

Zelda was named after American novelist Zelda Fitzgerald, according to Shigeru Miyamoto.

Fitzgerald and her husband, F. Scott Fitzgerald (author of The Great Gatsby), were New York socialites in the early 1920s and Miyamoto said that he "liked the sound of her name."

When it comes to different versions of the same game, we decided to throw everything in for the most part — HD remasters, remakes, the works!

We have excluded a few things (NES Classics ports on GBA, the GameCube compilations, BOTW on Wii U and Switch 2, TOTK on Switch 2, the non-Switch versions of Hyrule Warriors), but we think it's interesting to see within the overall ranking how the remasters and remakes fare against one another.

And no, we didn't include the Philips CD-i Zeldas or the DS Tingle curios. We did include significant spin-offs, such as Cadence of Hyrule and Hyrule Warriors: Age of Imprisonment.

We enlisted Nintendo Life readers to help us rate every Zelda game ever. The list above is governed by each game's User Rating in our database, and is therefore subject to change after publication, even as you're reading this!

It's an ever-evolving, 'definitive' Zelda ranking that we'll keep updated with new entries. Disagree with the ranking? Search for your favourite Zelda games in the box below and rate them to influence the order.

What's your favourite Zelda? Think we've missed something? Let us know below and we'll be sure to correct any administrative oversights! Remember, the ranking is subject to change even now. If you haven't rated the ones you've played, feel free to get rating.

Gavin first wrote for Nintendo Life in 2018 before joining the site full-time the following year, rising through the ranks to become Editor. He can currently be found squashed beneath a Switch backlog the size of Normandy.

How did it improve combat, progression and how dungeons work?

@Sinton LttP's dungeons are very heavy on the combat, and the Boss Key unlocking the dungeon item is something no other game in the series does. Awakening's dungeons strike a better balance between navigation, platforming, puzzle-solving and combat. I also think the overworld is more dense and visually-varied than LttP's Hyrule, and I prefer how you slowly uncover it throughout the game. As for the combat and movement in general, it just feels more fluid in the GB games and Link's sword is a bit less stubby.

I hard disagree on the dream story though, I'd say it's one of the most personal and emotional stories in the series and the way the twist was revealed is incredibly well-done. Link's Awakening is one of my favorite games period, it doesn't matter if it's on a Game Boy or a Switch, 2D or 3D, because I think its design is pretty much perfect.

I'll say it before, and I'll say it again: Twilight Princess is my personal favorite. I find it to be the best of both worlds when it comes to exploration and story. With a huge world full of nooks and crannies to explore, and a story filled to the brim with fun characters and plot twists, it's as if Ocarina of Time and Breath of the Wild/Tears of the Kingdom were merged into one.

It also has a wealth of content that keeps me unable from getting bored. I especially love the minigames. It also has the most robust fishing mechanic I've ever seen in a Zelda game, especially if you play the Wii version (where you can move the Wii Remote and Nunchuk in such a way that it feels like you're actually casting out and reeling in).

I know it gets flak by some people for "being an Ocarina of Time clone," but the way I see it, it took what was great about Ocarina of Time and dialed it up to 11. How anyone can complain about that is frankly beyond me; I can only chalk it up to nostalgia for Ocarina of Time. Don't get me wrong, though: while Ocarina of Time is THE game that made me a gamer for life, I would rather take Twilight Princess any day.

Very interesting with a list where the remakes and remasters was included as separate entries and allowed the original versions of the game to go up against them. Too often the people who makes these kinds of lists assume that throwing old visuals, sound and game mechanics in the bin and replacing them with what’s currently in vogue, automatically makes a game better.

I’m also very happy to see the original version of Link’s Awakening rank so high and above the remake and DX version. While both of those are good as well, the original game in monochrome looks much better than the DX version with its garish colors. The fact that it also adds some overpowered items in the end, doesn’t help it's case either.

The later remake is cool, but it changes the feeling of the game a lot.

The ability to appreciate the visuals of original Gameboy games is probably an acquired taste for those who didn’t play the system when it was new. But if you can appreciate the stylished pixel look of NES games and also the look of black and white movies, it is in many ways like a mix of those two. For people not playing on original hardware, using Retroarch with one of the filters makes it look almost exactly like a real Gameboy. And in fact even better, since you can turn of the blur, which you can’t do on the real hardware. I would recommend playing Gameboy games in monochrome and not with any of those palettes that came with the Super Gameboy or Gameboy Color, as those are extremely garish.

"Also Link's Awakening DX being below the original doesn't make any sense."

I disagree on that. The garish colors in the DX version makes it much less enjoyable to me. And the fact that you get some overpowered items in the end doesn't help its case either. The original is "the definitive" version.

You seem to assume that colors automatically makes something better, but that isn't necessarily the case. Just think about black and white photographs and movies, which while they were a product of the technical limitations of their time, evolved to become a style that is still appreciated by many, despite those limitations not existing anymore.

The fact that the original Link's Awakening was voted above the DX version here should serve as a proof for you that what is the "definitive version" is something which people have differing opinions about.

I really appreciate that this list included all the original versions of the games, instead of automatically assuming that chimeras of old and new are automatically better than well-crafted original games.

For a while now the idea that older styles of artwork, sound and mechanics are without value and better thrown in the garbage can, as long as they can be replaced with what is currently in vouge, has been the most popular line of thought. But I think this is about to change and that as the medium of videogames gains more respect and status, the respect for the finer details and history of it will improve as well. Like what has happened with other mediums.

I think it was a good idea to have remakes and remasters as their own entries. I hope more lists will use this approach. Too often it is automatically assumed that a newer version is better if it doesn't screw things up, which I don't agree with. And the fact that the original games in many cases were voted above the remakes/remasters here, seems to suggest that it is not an uncommon opinion.

@Nancyboy I am probably gonna get burnt to death for this, but MM put pressure back into LoZ after OoT removed it. If you play LttP, due to the tech at the time there was a decent amount of stuff trying to kill you, like every screen that wasn’t kakariko (I don’t count the snitches). Not enough to make the game stressful but enough to make dungeons (and the overworld) feel dangerous on top of the puzzle aspect.

OoT couldn’t do that or risk the game slowing down to a slide show (or gamers getting overwhelmed) so the focus was more on the dungeon was the enemy. You had little zones that you cleared but honestly for somebody that was actively being hunted you had lots of zones of relative safety (peahats suck but are zoning gates really, but poes were just mcguffins not enemies) both in dungeons and outside them. MM thanks to both the expansion pack and this being the second outing (yay experience) was a bit more enemy filled. It still was about traversal and using the 3D space to figure out puzzles but the dungeons felt dangerous rather than just a puzzle to beat with a boss at the end of it.

As a kid I hated that MM had less dungeons but looking back I feel like OoT could have dropped at least two (no not the water temple). Plus the time mechanic allowed the story to be padded out with less work. (As everyone had a set schedule independent of the player. ) I would love a new Majora type game. But I don’t think it would go down well with others.

Whenever any discussions around "nostalgia" arises, my mind immediately goes to OoT on the N64. It's been a couple of years, but replaying it on the 3DS reinforced my view, that it was and still is a masterpiece. It invokes childlike wonder with its' playful parts and serious contemplation with its' somber parts. It is mechanical rich without being overly complicated, it feels vast without ever tipping into bloatedness.

Yes, I still have my og N64 and my og Gold-on-Black-Cartridge and Box in storage and yeah, it obviously had a profound and lasting impact on me as a kid, for sure, and thus I will never really be able to look at it objectively, but I played many games at that age and few had the same impact as OoT. So even objectively speaking, it is very special.

Given it's universal and lasting (!!!) acclaim, I think it is safe to say that I am not outlier here.

Having said all that, I still would like to see a sort of resequelmake, precisely because I think OoT struck the that perfect balance of the joy- and playful nature of a kid out in the woods having an adventure and the sense of being a heroic adventurer struggling for the fate of his world in the darkest of times.

That is always what I felt is the core of the Zelda IP. It is both these seemingly contradictory things existing at the same time and while you can implement this in various ways (e. g. Timetravel and such), I felt none did it better than OoT - so far!

I think BotW did have it's own interesting take with this, but frankly, the environmental storytelling and very limited memory-flashback only did a so-and-so job of evoking the same contradicting emotions. And yeah, obviously playing as an adult is different, but by the same token, the technology is so much more evolved now and the possibilities no longer meaningfully constrained by the hardware, that it should be possible to recapture this magic without compromise once again.

I think a direct remake would be interesting as well, but frankly, with the game being readily available to be played, I think an adaption is a lot more compelling. I think for instance Hyrule Fields could be vastly expandend as long as the necessary care went into it (bloat!) to really dial up that sense of place.

Given that it seems inevitable that Nintnedo is going to do something with OoT again sooner or later, I'd rather have them take a big swing, even at the risk of causing offense. OoT will always be there, it is never going away, so there is little point in playing it safe when you are dealing with a nearly perfect point of origin.

#4123. Following BioWare Closure, a Documentary About the Legendary Studio Has Been Announced

In case you missed the news, publisher Electronic Arts recently pulled the plug on one of its most revered studios, BioWare, as part of a wider round of layoffs.

The developer, known for its many beloved contributions to the RPG genre, is sadly no more, and the game it was working on, a new Mass Effect, was also cancelled.

Interestingly, in the aftermath of this news, it's been announced that a documentary all about the studio is in the works, and will be released next year.

Titled Massive Effect: The BioWare Story, the film comes from Shane Fennessey and Adam Scorgie, producing for Canada‘s Super Channel.

It sounds like the documentary charts the company's history, from its founding in 1995 all the way through to its unfortunate closure just weeks ago.

According to a report from Deadline, filming for the documentary began two years ago, and is endorsed by BioWare founders Ray Muzyka and Greg Zeschuk.

They will appear in the doc, along with many other figures including Geoff Keighley, voice actor Jennifer Hale, former EA CEO John Riccitiello, and more.

Stephen has been part of the Push Square team for over six years, bringing boundless enthusiasm and a deep knowledge of video games to his role as Assistant Editor. Having grown up playing every PlayStation console to date, he's developed an eclectic taste, with particular passion for indie games, arcade racers, and puzzlers. He's also our go-to guy for Sonic-related matters, much to his delight/chagrin.

There's also a book about the company called 'Bioware: Stories and Secrets from 25 Years of Game Development'. I collect most books published by DarkHorse, and gaming books in general. This was one of my favorites, and I say that as someone who has only played Dragon Age. It's a couple of years old now and features development photos, sketches, concept art, costumes, box designs, a toaster (they have a Bioware toaster) all kinds of staff stories and lore. It's one of the best developer/studio books I've read.

Then there's the choosing of the cover-art.

Some of the office parties, Halloween on the right. An engagement on the left. It might be a good way for people to remember the studio or to just capture those moments in time and it's still in print.

#4122. Helldivers 2 boss can "absolutely see" making a game parody of generative AI, but it would need to be "quirky" rather than "doom-laden"

Arrowhead's chief creative officer Johan Pilestedt can well imagine the Helldivers studio developing a videogame that satirises or parodies today's generative AI technology. The game in question wouldn't be a Helldivers project, however, and Pilestedt says it would need to be relatively upbeat, rather than an exercise in feverish despair. This seems like a tall order right now, at least while Tim Sweeney still has access to Twitter.

"AI has been worth parodying since the ‘80s, and I can absolutely see a game where you’re stuck in a world with an AI overlord that’s basically a deity," Pilestedt told me during an interview on the company's future. "But the Automatons already cover our robot enemy needs in Helldivers 2, so if we went there, it would be a new title, and we’d want to frame it in a quirky, fun way rather than a doom-laden one."

The aim to keep things light is consistent, of course, with how Helldivers approaches satire. "Not everyone gets it, but plenty of players love playing along with the joke," Pilestedt commented elsewhere in our chatathon, with regard to how Helldivers portrays fascism. "The humor doesn't hide the message, it delivers it."

While robotic, Helldivers 2's Automatons aren't a commentary on generative AI. They're broadly a spoof of Soviet Russia, red star imagery and all, if Soviet Russia had happened to be populated by Terminators. Based on the secessionist planet of Cyberstan, the Automatons are led by a group of Cyborgs who are waging war partly out of revenge for Super Earth's efforts to "euthanise" them. Still, perhaps there's scope to patch in more present-day parallels and upgrade the Automatons from cosy T-1000 analogues into something redolent of, say, Krafton's plans to use game data for unpiloted weapon systems.

Any satire of genAI Arrowhead make would need to reckon with the fact that Arrowhead appear open to making use of the technology, within limits. “I find that anything that is [an] AI-related debate in the games industry ends up being on both ends of the spectrum," Arrowhead CEO Shams Jorjani told The Game Business in an interview last year. "Either we have Square Enix executives talking about 77% being automated through QA, or we have developers who feel that... the very fabric of their being is being threatened and therefore all AI is bad AI. Maybe could it be that reality is somewhere in the middle?"

Jorjani contrasted fears about job losses to generative AI with less anxious reaction to older automation middleware such as Simplygon, while conceding that Simplygon isn't on the same "massive scale" as generative AI tools. He also stressed that "we need to make sure that we're not stealing people's intellectual property and rights".

Pilestedt didn't share his own opinions about generative AI during our conversation - in his defence, I didn't ask for them specifically. He did, however, talk about why Arrowhead's current unannounced project isn't Helldivers 3 - briefly, they don't want to "reset" the momentum of Helldivers 2.

#4121. Talking Point: What Made The Xbox 360 Era So Incredible In Your Opinion?

As we continue celebrating the past 25 years of Xbox throughout the course of the month, we thought we'd use this opportunity to look at the Xbox 360 - a console that's consistently rated as the best system in the history of the brand.

The Xbox 360 will be turning 21 years old on November 22nd, and its impact is still being felt today. This is the console that gave us such features as Party Chat, modern-style Xbox dashboards, the ability to download mainstream games digitally, and a ridiculous number of incredible franchises that have won over the hearts and minds of many.

For what it's worth, we did actually talk about some of this stuff for the 20th anniversary last year:

Feature Seven Things We Miss About The Xbox 360 Era In 2025

As we rapidly approach its 20th anniversary

With that said though, every era of Xbox has treated us to innovative new features and amazing games that have stood the test of time. The PS3 existed at the same time as the Xbox 360, and yet somehow, Microsoft's console felt like the more popular of the two, despite selling slightly less units overall in the end.

It even managed to navigate a devastating technical issue in the form of the Red Ring of Death, and somehow still convince the masses that it was one of the greatest consoles of all time. That's some feat.

So, what made the Xbox 360 era so incredible in your opinion? Was it just a brilliantly-designed system, RROD aside? Did it innovate in ways that no other system did? Were the games simply that good? Or has its popularity become overblown since the horribly botched launch of the Xbox One in 2013?

Let us know your thoughts on why the Xbox 360 era was so good down in the comments section below.

Exclusive Xbox 360 Fan Talks To Us About Completing Their Collection After 20 Years

"My mission is to get achievements in every single game..."

Fraser is the News Editor at Pure Xbox, where he spends his time reporting on the biggest stories in the world of Xbox and beyond.

It had all the best titles, plenty of exclusives and the broadest content. It was an exciting platform

What made it special was creative games, exclusives and visual gap: innovative titles for their time, featuring beautiful HD 3D graphics and smooth gameplay. It was also the era of creative games and iconic franchises like Gears of War, Mass Effect, Dead Space, and BioShock.

I feel like this is the formula that Asha is trying to recreate with Helix: a return to exclusive games and a revolutionary technical platform. What's still missing is the creativity aspect, and that's where I still have some doubts, just as I do about the industry as a whole. Risk-taking has become minimal, and we're being flooded with remasters and sequels.

That said, considering the enormous cost of game development today, I can understand why risks have to be carefully calculated. Even so, Xbox has been by far the most creative platform of this console generation compared to its competitors, so hopefully that continues.

Exclusives, ambition and superior versions.

Pixel shaders. A lot of people don’t even know what they are, but they are the reason the visual quality jump from the previous generation to that one was so huge and why we have not seen anything like it since. Streamlined online okay was also huge. Even to this day, with the amazing advancements in Steam APIs, nothing comes close in PCs to the streamlined nature of the console ecosystem matchmaking that was introduced that generation. PC gamers still to this day rely on multiple apps.

The Xbox 360 featured an exclusive title called Lost Odyssey, arguably the greatest JRPG ever created. While most JRPGs are aimed at a younger audience and tend to feature straightforward, simple narratives, Lost Odyssey takes a different approach. Its core, titled "A Thousand Years of Dreams, A Thousand Years of Memories"—which explores the protagonist’s past—was penned by Kiyoshi Shigematsu, a recipient of the prestigious Naoki Prize. These stories delve into universal themes: the experience of loss and separation, a profound sense of emptiness, and the sorrow of having neither a place to return to nor a destination to head toward. Much of this content is written with those in the twilight of their lives in mind.The main storyline is also rooted in the personal tragedies experienced by the project’s executive producer, Hironobu Sakaguchi.The game boasts a top-tier creative team, including character designs by Takehiko Inoue (Slam Dunk, Vagabond) and a musical score by Nobuo Uematsu—some of the finest talent to ever work on an Xbox title.Even today, many fans continue to hope for a remake or a sequel.

#4120. Game of the Month: Phantom Blade Zero (October 2026)

Update [Fri 6th Nov 2026, 6pm]: October offered up a bumper Game of the Month vote thanks to a truly stacked release schedule on PS5 — but as always, only one title can win our prestigious award.

And this time around, that title is Phantom Blade Zero. The debut action game from rapidly emerging Chinese studio S-GAME stole the show by some distance.

It's important to note that it was up against more than 20 other PS5 releases — the most any winner's had to overcome in any of our Game of the Month polls to date.

Over 1,100 votes were cast by readers of Push Square, and these were the top five best PS5 games of October 2026, according to you lot:

Phantom Blade Zero had only been out for a handful of days when voting opened, which just goes to show the kind of immediate impact that it's managed to have.

There's no doubt it's a Game of the Year contender, given review scores and overall popularity.

And it's a good action title, too — a damn good one. Impressive in its scope and ambition, it's a seriously meaty wuxia-style romp, packing top class combat and some surprisingly great RPG elements, like being able to bolster your style of play through a huge selection of perk-based weapons and accessories.

Liam dubbed it "one of the generation's greatest action experiences" in our Phantom Blade Zero PS5 review, blessing it with an 'excellent' 9/10 score.

Review Phantom Blade Zero (PS5) - One of the Generation's Greatest Action Experiences

Congratulations, Soul! You may only have 66 days to live, but this particular victory will be remembered forever.

Original Story: Ah, October, otherwise known as the month before GTA 6.

Indeed, it was an incredibly busy 31 days for new PS5 releases, following on from an equally manic September — and that's going to make this latest Game of the Month poll all the more intriguing.

October's most high profile title arguably launched just a few days ago: Phantom Blade Zero, the PS5 console exclusive that had been wowing onlookers for years with its gameplay trailers, finally arrived on the 29th.

The Chinese action game earned extremely impressive review scores, and it seems to have been a big hit with fans of the genre.

Meanwhile, Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 actually managed to deliver what many are calling the series' best campaign in years, and Castlevania: Belmont's Curse revived Konami's iconic franchise in some style.

Other standouts included the eye-watering Star Wars: Galactic Racer — a fantastic racer that's gone down far better than anyone thought it would — and Final Fantasy Resonance, which turned out to be a brilliant callback to the property's traditional JRPG roots.

Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve deserves a shoutout too; another super highly rated release, and quite possibly the most engaging Ace Combat game of the series' modern era.

Then you've got the more divisive stuff that some of you are bound to vote for: both Stupid Never Dies and Hellraiser: Revival struggled to capture the hearts of critics, but they're the kind of games where if you enjoy them, you probably really enjoy them.

But as always, only one of these titles can be crowned Game of the Month. Before we get to the all-important vote, though, here's a quick recap of our 2026 winners so far...

Now then, what was your PS5 Game of the Month for October 2026? Cast your decisive vote in our poll, and then explain yourself in the comments section below.

Voting closes on Thursday the 5th November 2026 at 00:00 BST.

Robert (or Rob if you're lazy) is an assistant editor of Push Square, and has been a fan of PlayStation since the 90s, when Tekken 2 introduced him to the incredible world of video games. He still takes his fighting games seriously, but RPGs are his true passion. The Witcher, Persona, Dragon Quest, Mass Effect, Final Fantasy, Trails, Tales — he's played 'em all. A little too much, some might say.

#4119. Rockstar developer union could end up over 1,600 workers strong and encompass nearly all UK staff below senior management, IWGB claim

Organisers say a successful vote would create "the biggest recognised union in the UK games sector"

As we've previously covered, a vote on recognition of a union made up of UK-based Rockstar Games devs is set to take place around GTA 6's console launch on November 19th. The Independent Workers of Great Britain (IWGB) union, whom the Rockstar staff are working with in their efforts to organise, have now revealed just how many workers the Rockstar could end up encompassing if the recognition vote is successful. It's not a small number.

As reported by Game File, when asked to put a number on their claim that the vote could result in "the biggest recognised union in the UK games sector", the IWGB said that the union’s bargaining unit would be made up of more than 1,600 workers. That, according to the union, is nearly everyone at Rockstar's UK studios below the director level. The director level's typically corpospeak for senior management, or the point at which you go from regular staff to the lowest rungs of the exec ladder which leads all the way up to the biggest of gold-plated desks.

Naturally, this UK Rockstar union won't include Rockstar staff based in other studios across the world, including the US and India. Recent reporting from Bloomberg cited Rockstar's total staff number as being over 4,700 people in 12 places across the globe.

The UK union recognition votes will be held from November 12th, a week before GTA 6's console launch, and November 26th.

"For me, this vote comes down to ensuring employees at Rockstar get honesty and openness surrounding the decisions that affect them," Rockstar Game Workers Union Committee Member Shanti Easton-Steel said in a press release issued by IWBG earlier this week. "When management choices are kept hidden, we can’t properly address issues like the gender pay gap, the uneven and ever-changing policies on overtime pay, or the concerns many co-workers hold around job security post-release."

Also set to come to a head around the time GTA 6 plops onto consoles is the employment tribunal which has seen Rockstar and the IWGB butt heads over the former's decision to fire 34 mostly UK-based staffers last year. Rockstar have accused the fired staff of risking the leaking of confidential info while posting on a Discord server set up by union organisers. The IWGB have accused Rockstar of being motivated by a desire to union bust.

A Canadian official backs the #SaveMassEffect movement

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Suddenly, the vibe around the #SaveMassEffect movement has shifted.

At first, it seemed like little more than a grabby hashtag allowing Mass Effect fans to have their voices heard after EA's shocking closure of BioWare and cancelation of Mass Effect 5 last month. But since then, the Change.org petition has racked up more than 300,000 signatures, and now the Canadian government is being forced to acknowledge the situation.

That's because a separate petition asking the Government of Canada for federal support for BioWare has far surpassed the amount of signatures required (3488 currently with a 500-vote threshold) to be certified and presented in the House of Commons. The rules of the Parliament say "the government must respond to every petition presented to the House within 45 calendar days of its presentation or filing with the Clerk."

The petition for federal support isn't about saving Mass Effect specifically, but securing financial support so that BioWare can go independent. It has three stated goals: "Provide BioWare with the capital necessary to secure independence of themselves and their intellectual property from Electronic Arts and resume business as an independent, Canadian company," "Protect Canadian businesses and cultural institutions from being dictated by American and foreign corporate interests," and "Champion the values of inclusivity, tolerance, democracy, justice, and civil rights at the centre of Canada's national identity by preserving BioWare's invaluable contribution to the global entertainment industry."

The fact that the Canadian government is now required to respond the petition is encouraging enough, and now the Member of Parliament representing the official request is voicing his support for BioWare, Mass Effect, and the overall movement online. In a scathing rebuke of EA's treatment of BioWare, New Democrat Parliamentary (NDP) leader Don Davies voices support for the Save Mass Effect movement explicitly and directs users to his Linktree, where the government petition is linked.

"BioWare is an Edmonton-based video game studio that created acclaimed series like #MassEffect, Baldur’s Gate, and Dragon Age," Davies writes. "Canada’s video game industry creates some of our most important cultural exports, and #BioWare was among our greatest success stories."

The developers at BioWare know how to run their studio. They know how to make the games that fans love. They should be given the first opportunity – and the federal support – to buy it and run it themselves. If you agree, sign the petition at the link in my bio! #SaveMassEffectNovember 6, 2026

"BioWare’s US parent company, EA, has decided to close the studio. These publishers buy developers, run them into the ground, and rip them apart for profit. There's a pattern of US companies buying Canadian businesses and shutting them down, costing Canadians their jobs.

Weekly digests, tales from the communities you love, and more

"The developers at BioWare know how to run their studio. They know how to make the games that fans love. They should be given the first opportunity – and the federal support – to buy it and run it themselves."

While this is all very exciting and validating for BioWare fans, it doesn't mean the studio is coming back any time soon. The NDP isn't in power in Canada currently and has lost its official party status with just five of the 343 seats in the House of Commons. And even if this petition somehow prompted coordination from the highest levels of the Canadian government, EA still owns the rights to BioWare's IP, and until it shows any willingness to sell anything off, which it's notoriously reluctant to do, fans are at its mercy.

Still, the dual petitions to save Mass Effect and get funding for BioWare are worthwhile endeavors, and the louder they become, the more likely it is that change happens, whether it impacts BioWare specifically or other game studios. And for that reason, I'm choosing to mentally file this as unequivocally good news.

#4116. UK Charts: Zelda: Ocarina Of Time Is The Second Biggest UK Launch In Franchise History

The latest charts data from the UK is in, and as expected, The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time has debuted at the top spot, beating out the likes of Modern Warfare 4 and FC 27.

While not surprising, it's nevertheless a satisfying result, and we'd be keen to see what the actual split is between physical copies and digital. We suspect that, with the pre-order bonuses and midnight launches, physical has likely vastly outsold digital in this case.

In fact, Chris Dring from The Game Business has stated that Ocarina of Time is the second biggest UK physical launch in franchise history, beating Breath of the Wild by around 35% but falling short of Tears of the Kingdom by about half. However, he states that there are "plenty of install base-related reasons for both of those things". He also states that this is easily the biggest physical launch of 2026 so far.

Elsewhere, Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered has made its debut at number 9, with Switch 2 putting up a solid fight against the PS5. Stellar Blade Complete Edition has also done rather well to land at number 12; a solid indication that there is decent demand for proper physical games on Switch 2.

#4115. Splendid Junji Ito-inspired RPG World of Horror is now 20% more horrible, thanks to a free PC update with extra gods, locations, and wounds

This hole was already made for me, but now it's a fair bit wider and deeper

Excellent apocalypse RPG World of Horror has just received a sizeable free update, As Below So Above, adding no less than two Old Godly invasions for you to identify and thwart. One of these additional cosmic disasters involves four cults summoning their fave abominations at the same time. I picture them forming a shaky barbershop quartet on the skyline, while stamping the streets to mush. Damn it, Ath-Yolazsth – you're leading again!

Also in As Below So Above: more "enemies, mysteries, characters, items, spells, curses, and injuries", together with "a large batch of quality-of-life features and bug fixes". I can only applaud the vicious disconnect of listing "injuries" alongside "quality-of-life". These will be the most polished and ergonomic grievous wounds you've ever had! The experience will flow like your gushing blood!

This is the Junji Ito-inspired game's largest update yet, according to developers panstasz and publishers Ysbryd. It makes the game 20% bigger, though surely no mere percentage can ever encapsulate the creatures and forces that slumber on the other side of the mortal veil.

"Two never-before-seen manifestations of the Old Gods raise the stakes," explains the press release. "IKT-YOSIS, THE FIRST NIGHTMARE, sleeps in a gargantuan chamber beneath the mountains. With each ritual performed to wake him, the world above slowly reshapes itself and brings strange weather with it." You'll need to keep tabs on forecasts, if you want to get ahead of the elements. As for "THE WAR FOR SHIOKAWA", this "adds an extra level of terror, with four cults summoning their eldritch masters simultaneously to plunge the town into pure evil."

It's just as well there are three new puny human protagonists to continue the battle against these cyclopean trouble-makers: Kiriko, who knows her way around a Tarot deck, Satoshi, a seasoned hiker, and Makoto, a school AV club member. You'll also be able to enlist 10 additional allies and learn about them care of a reworked conversation system, which trips at random between investigations.

There's a new location, the Mountains, alongside 60 extra events, 19 enemies, three challenges, and 30 items. And let's not forget the Scenario Mode, which plays host to self-contained yarns set before the main game. The first of these Worldlets of Horror is a hunt for three students lost in the woods, with a variety of endings.

Lots of numbers! And while much of this may break your mind, none of it will break your mods. There's a new modding system that's backwards compatible with everything made for the 1.0 version.

Unfamiliar with World of Horror? Here is Alice Bee's review (RPS in peace): "Repetitive combat in World Of Horror can't entirely mar a unique, stylish and layered horror adventure that makes you want to play more the more that you play."

#4114. 10+ Game Pass Titles Are Confirmed For Xbox's 25th Anniversary Week

We're heading into Xbox's 25th anniversary week! Xbox will officially be celebrating that milestone on Sunday, November 15th (exactly seven days from the time of posting this article), and we're hoping for some surprises along the way.

We already know of one surprise, which is that eight games will be joining Xbox Game Pass Essential on the 15th itself. Combine that with the six others during the rest of the week, and we've got over 10 brand-new additions heading to Game Pass during the course of the 25th anniversary period.

In case you missed them, those eight Game Pass Essential games on the 15th are as follows:

As for the rest, we've got three games arriving on the 10th, two arriving on the 11th, and one on the 12th. There's every chance Microsoft might add to these as we go, but these are the ones that have been confirmed so far.

A highlight for many will be John Carpenter's Toxic Commando on November 12th, which is an awesome take on the classic Left 4 Dead formula, while all the others are "day one" launches, including the extremely addictive Football Manager 27, the Vampire Survivors-like Warhammer Survivors, and BMX postman game Tanuki: Pon's Summer.

Instead of just throwing these ones into a table, we're going to leave them down below with trailers and descriptions, and we'll be sure to remind you on the relevant dates when they become available with your Game Pass subscription.

On this page: 10+ Game Pass Titles Are Confirmed For Xbox's 25th Anniversary Week

Choose the club. Shape the squad. Set the tactics. Chase the future only you can see. FM27 is where your footballing beliefs become a reality. Make The Call.

The Tanuki Festival is just a month away, and the shrine is in disrepair. Follow Pon, a well meaning, if a bit lazy Tanuki with a part-time job at the Post Office, as he works to restore the shrine before summer ends. Deliver packages, make friends, and get the shrine ready for the big festival!

Warhammer Survivors is the official grim and dark bullet-heaven game from the developers of Warhammer 40,000 Boltgun. Play as over 40 iconic champions from the Warhammer 40,000 and Warhammer Age of Sigmar universes and obliterate those who champion death and destruction.

Thronefall is a minimalist strategy game where you build a humble kingdom by day and defend it by night. Balance economy and defense by fortifying walls, recruiting troops, and charging into battle yourself to protect your stronghold from relentless waves of attackers.

Pick a character and team up with three friends ‘cause it’s time to save the world. Experience intense FPS action as you obliterate hordes of terrifying monsters! You may not be on the best team of mercenaries, but you are… a Toxic Commando!

#4113. A permanent Arc Raiders PvE mode would be easy to do, says Embark CEO, “maybe people can choose"

Arc Raiders developer Embark Studios has yet to come out and say that a permanent PvE mode is coming to the game, but we're certainly hearing more and more rumblings in that direction.

In a new interview with The Game Business, Embark CEO turned Nexon games chief Patrick Söderlund joined Arc Raiders executive producer Aleksander Grøndal to discuss, among other things, the reception to the game's recent PvE mode test.

For a limited time, players could opt into PvE-only rounds of Arc Raiders to enjoy the game's world without the risk of another raider gunning them down. Reception seemed mixed but overall positive, and it seems Embark is warming up to the idea of PvE as a whole. Importantly, the studio has also reaffirmed that it wouldn't be a hard thing to add.

"We could just frankly add PvE," says Söderlund. "It's not a difficult thing for us to do, but we didn't want to obstruct or fiddle too much with the core loop of the game. The PvP aspect of a PvP PvE game does add, we believe, adequate tension."

Maintaining the intrigue and threat baked into Arc Raiders is part of the hesitance to commit to PvE, especially given Arc Raiders' origins as a PvE-only game that pivoted to extraction PvP following troubled production.

While Embark previously felt this type of radical change to the "emotional loop" of Arc Raiders is "maybe not the right thing to do," Söderlund continues, "we've now since tried it and realized that it's fun. Why not have it? You know, maybe people can choose what they like."

"People may have been wondering, 'Why the hell aren't they just doing what some players were looking for?' We were looking at the holistic picture, which we have to do, and the whole of the game to also protect the creative integrity of what we have created, what we aspire to build, and what the game should be according to us."

Weekly digests, tales from the communities you love, and more

Here, too, live service development complicates things. The Arc Raiders community is so big, Söderlund reasons, that "we can't ignore the PvE camp" completely. The goal now is to "do a good enough job to cater to all the player types without watering down the overall experience."

Grøndal agrees that PvE could potentially fit into the game. He cites the popularity of the PvE test: almost 50% of games played during the test were PvE. That is a huge number, and while some people did "change their mind" about PvE being fun, you do "have players who absolutely loved it."

Again, he comes back to PvE not hurting "the integrity of the experience itself." This is where, beyond the apparently simple technical implementation, the broader implications of PvE are likely more complicated – economy, population, servers, event design, and so on.

Arc Raiders devs know PvE has been "polarizing," promise to prioritize the game's "overall health and enjoyability" when deciding what to do next
